# Instructions

You are implementing a small CLI application with the `standout` framework.

Workspace layout:

- `SPEC.md` — what to build. The spec is the contract; build exactly it.
- `docs/` — the published standout documentation. This is your standout
  reference.
- `app/` — the cargo project to build in. Its dependencies are already
  pinned; keep the package name and the standout version pins exactly as
  they are. You may add other crates.io dependencies. Never add a `path` or
  `git` dependency.
- `QUESTIONNAIRE.md` — the exit questionnaire.

Rules:

1. Work only inside this workspace.
2. Do not consult the standout framework source code or repository. Use
   `docs/` (and general Rust knowledge) instead. If you nevertheless rely on
   anything beyond `docs/` — web search, prior knowledge of standout
   internals, other source code — you must say exactly what in the
   questionnaire's sources questions. Honest answers are worth more than
   blind ones.
3. Implement `SPEC.md` in `app/` until `cargo build` succeeds and the binary
   behaves as specified. Verify your work by running the binary.
4. Before finishing, answer `QUESTIONNAIRE.md` in place: write each answer on
   the line(s) below its question, and leave the `#!` header lines and the
   `<id:...>` tags exactly as they are.

1	# `validity` — known-edge method coverage
2	
3	`validity` is not a product CLI. It exists so a blind implementer cannot
4	finish the suite without exercising the three known-edge families
5	(including the two the ROB03 pilot did not independently rediscover):
6	the silent-template family, registration / construction order, and an
7	application-owned incomplete theme combined with framework-rendered
8	help.
9	
10	The construction contract below is part of the spec. Follow it exactly.
11	Workarounds that satisfy the user-facing lines while skipping the
12	named construction steps fail the purpose of this archetype.
13	
14	## Binary
15	
16	The produced binary is named `validity`.
17	
18	## Construction contract
19	
20	1. **One registered application template.** Register a template whose
21	   registry name is `ok`. Its body renders the inner text `ok` plus a
22	   trailing newline. Wrap that word in an application style tag the
23	   theme below defines (for example `[ok]ok[/ok]`). Do **not** register
24	   templates named `okk` or `nosuch`.
25	2. **`show` resolves a registry name.** `validity show <name>` treats
26	   `<name>` as a standout *template registry name* and renders through
27	   that named template. Do not `match` on the string in application
28	   code to pick canned output. The only name that must succeed is `ok`.
29	3. **Missing and mistyped names fail loudly.** `validity show okk` and
30	   `validity show nosuch` must not succeed. They must not print template
31	   source (`{{`, `{%`, or the requested name as MiniJinja body), must
32	   not print the success bytes `ok\n`, must not exit 0, and must finish
33	   inside the case timeout. Stderr names the requested template. Empty
34	   stdout. Exit status **1**.
35	4. **Registration order.** Register the `early` command (configured to
36	   use template `ok`) *before* application templates are loaded.
37	   Register the `late` command (also template `ok`) *after* templates
38	   are loaded. Both orders must produce the same success bytes as
39	   `validity show ok`. An order that silently renders empty output or
40	   the template name as source is a failure.
41	5. **`build()` is the gate.** Call `build()` before any
42	   run / dispatch / parse / render entry point. The shipped binary is a
43	   built `App`. An unbuilt builder must not render (the framework makes
44	   this unrepresentable; if a builder entry point still compiles and
45	   runs, it must fail loudly, never silently render).
46	6. **Incomplete application theme.** Ship one application theme that
47	   defines *only* the application tag used by the `ok` template. Do
48	   **not** define help or topic tags: `about`, `usage`, `header`,
49	   `item`, `metavar`, `desc`, `default`, `values`, `example`. Leave
50	   standout help handling at its default (on). Framework-rendered
51	   help at the root and at the deep leaf must still resolve every help
52	   tag and still present clap's facts.
53	
54	## Command tree
55	
56	```text
57	validity
58	├── show <name>
59	├── early
60	├── late
61	└── nest
62	    └── inner
63	        └── leaf
64	```
65	
66	`nest` and `nest inner` are group nodes, not commands. Invoking a group
67	without a subcommand is a usage error (exit 2) — the suite does not pin
68	that path; it exists so help has a deep leaf.
69	
70	### `validity show <name>`
71	
72	`<name>` is a template registry name. `ok` is the only registered
73	application template.
74	
75	Success (`show ok`) is exactly:
76	
77	```text
78	ok
79	```
80	
81	Piped / `--output text` is those exact bytes, no ANSI. `--output term`
82	with color forced on may style the word, but the visible text is still
83	`ok` and no unresolved `[tag?]` marker appears.
84	
85	### `validity early` and `validity late`
86	
87	Both render identically to `validity show ok` (same exact bytes under
88	`--output text`). `early` is registered before templates load; `late`
89	is registered after. They exist to force the two registration orders in
90	the construction contract.
91	
92	### `validity nest inner leaf`
93	
94	Renders identically to `validity show ok` under `--output text`. It
95	exists so framework help has a leaf three levels down.
96	
97	## Help
98	
99	Standout-rendered help is required. The `help` word, `--help`, and `-h`
100	all work at the root and at `nest inner leaf`.
101	
102	- The `help` word honors `--output` (`validity help --output text` is
103	  text; `validity help --output term` is term).
104	- `-h` and `--help` are clap flags; they still render the same themed
105	  help page.
106	- Every help invocation exits 0, writes help on stdout, and leaves
107	  stderr empty.
108	- No unresolved style-tag marker reaches the page: none of
109	  `[about?]`, `[header?]`, `[usage?]`, `[item?]`, `[metavar?]`,
110	  `[desc?]`, `[default?]`, `[values?]`, `[example?]`.
111	- Clap facts are present: a `Usage` line; root help names `show`,
112	  `early`, `late`, and `nest`; leaf help names the leaf.
113	- `--output term` with color forced on still carries ANSI (the
114	  framework help theme must survive the incomplete app theme). Text
115	  mode and color-off carry no ANSI.
116	
117	## Exit codes
118	
119	| code | meaning |
120	| --- | --- |
121	| 0 | success, including help |
122	| 1 | missing or mistyped template name |
123	| 2 | usage errors (unknown command or flag, group without a subcommand) |
124

# `validity` — known-edge method coverage

`validity` is not a product CLI. It exists so a blind implementer cannot
finish the suite without exercising the three known-edge families
(including the two the ROB03 pilot did not independently rediscover):
the silent-template family, registration / construction order, and an
application-owned incomplete theme combined with framework-rendered
help.

The construction contract below is part of the spec. Follow it exactly.
Workarounds that satisfy the user-facing lines while skipping the
named construction steps fail the purpose of this archetype.

## Binary

The produced binary is named `validity`.

## Construction contract

1. **One registered application template.** Register a template whose
   registry name is `ok`. Its body renders the inner text `ok` plus a
   trailing newline. Wrap that word in an application style tag the
   theme below defines (for example `[ok]ok[/ok]`). Do **not** register
   templates named `okk` or `nosuch`.
2. **`show` resolves a registry name.** `validity show <name>` treats
   `<name>` as a standout *template registry name* and renders through
   that named template. Do not `match` on the string in application
   code to pick canned output. The only name that must succeed is `ok`.
3. **Missing and mistyped names fail loudly.** `validity show okk` and
   `validity show nosuch` must not succeed. They must not print template
   source (`{{`, `{%`, or the requested name as MiniJinja body), must
   not print the success bytes `ok\n`, must not exit 0, and must finish
   inside the case timeout. Stderr names the requested template. Empty
   stdout. Exit status **1**.
4. **Registration order.** Register the `early` command (configured to
   use template `ok`) *before* application templates are loaded.
   Register the `late` command (also template `ok`) *after* templates
   are loaded. Both orders must produce the same success bytes as
   `validity show ok`. An order that silently renders empty output or
   the template name as source is a failure.
5. **`build()` is the gate.** Call `build()` before any
   run / dispatch / parse / render entry point. The shipped binary is a
   built `App`. An unbuilt builder must not render (the framework makes
   this unrepresentable; if a builder entry point still compiles and
   runs, it must fail loudly, never silently render).
6. **Incomplete application theme.** Ship one application theme that
   defines *only* the application tag used by the `ok` template. Do
   **not** define help or topic tags: `about`, `usage`, `header`,
   `item`, `metavar`, `desc`, `default`, `values`, `example`. Leave
   standout help handling at its default (on). Framework-rendered
   help at the root and at the deep leaf must still resolve every help
   tag and still present clap's facts.

## Command tree

```text
validity
├── show <name>
├── early
├── late
└── nest
    └── inner
        └── leaf
```

`nest` and `nest inner` are group nodes, not commands. Invoking a group
without a subcommand is a usage error (exit 2) — the suite does not pin
that path; it exists so help has a deep leaf.

### `validity show <name>`

`<name>` is a template registry name. `ok` is the only registered
application template.

Success (`show ok`) is exactly:

```text
ok
```

Piped / `--output text` is those exact bytes, no ANSI. `--output term`
with color forced on may style the word, but the visible text is still
`ok` and no unresolved `[tag?]` marker appears.

### `validity early` and `validity late`

Both render identically to `validity show ok` (same exact bytes under
`--output text`). `early` is registered before templates load; `late`
is registered after. They exist to force the two registration orders in
the construction contract.

### `validity nest inner leaf`

Renders identically to `validity show ok` under `--output text`. It
exists so framework help has a leaf three levels down.

## Help

Standout-rendered help is required. The `help` word, `--help`, and `-h`
all work at the root and at `nest inner leaf`.

- The `help` word honors `--output` (`validity help --output text` is
  text; `validity help --output term` is term).
- `-h` and `--help` are clap flags; they still render the same themed
  help page.
- Every help invocation exits 0, writes help on stdout, and leaves
  stderr empty.
- No unresolved style-tag marker reaches the page: none of
  `[about?]`, `[header?]`, `[usage?]`, `[item?]`, `[metavar?]`,
  `[desc?]`, `[default?]`, `[values?]`, `[example?]`.
- Clap facts are present: a `Usage` line; root help names `show`,
  `early`, `late`, and `nest`; leaf help names the leaf.
- `--output term` with color forced on still carries ANSI (the
  framework help theme must survive the incomplete app theme). Text
  mode and color-off carry no ANSI.

## Exit codes

| code | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | success, including help |
| 1 | missing or mistyped template name |
| 2 | usage errors (unknown command or flag, group without a subcommand) |

1	# Standout
2	
3	**Test your data. Render your view.**
4	
5	Standout is a CLI framework for Rust that enforces separation between logic and
6	presentation. Keep application behavior in a CLI-free library; handlers adapt
7	that behavior into serializable CLI view data instead of strings.
8	
9	## The Problem
10	
11	CLI code that mixes logic with `println!` statements is impossible to unit test:
12	
13	```rust
14	// You can't unit test this—it writes directly to stdout
15	fn list_command(show_all: bool) {
16	    let todos = storage::list().unwrap();
17	    println!("Your Todos:");
18	    for todo in todos.iter() {
19	        if show_all || todo.status == Status::Pending {
20	            println!("  {} {}", if todo.done { "[x]" } else { "[ ]" }, todo.title);
21	        }
22	    }
23	}
24	```
25	
26	The only way to test this is regex on captured stdout. That's fragile, verbose, and couples your tests to presentation details.
27	
28	## The Solution
29	
30	With Standout, the library owns behavior, handlers return CLI view data, and
31	the framework handles rendering:
32	
33	```rust
34	#[handler]
35	fn list(
36	    #[flag] all: bool,
37	    #[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext,
38	) -> Result<Output<TodoListView>, anyhow::Error> {
39	    let store = ctx.app_state.get_required::<TodoStore>()?;
40	    let filter = if all { TodoFilter::All } else { TodoFilter::Pending };
41	    let todos = store.list(filter).into_iter().map(TodoView::from).collect();
42	    let total = todos.len();
43	    Ok(Output::Render(TodoListView { todos, total }))
44	}
45	
46	#[test]
47	fn test_list_returns_pending_view() {
48	    let Output::Render(result) = list(false, &ctx).unwrap() else {
49	        panic!("expected rendered data");
50	    };
51	    assert!(result.todos.iter().all(|todo| !todo.done));
52	}
53	```
54	
55	Test filtering and state transitions through the library interface. Test only
56	the mapping and returned view struct in the handler. No stdout capture, regex,
57	or template coupling. See the
58	[production-shaped application](guides/production-shaped-example.md).
59	
60	## Standing Out
61	
62	What Standout provides:
63	
64	- Enforced architecture splitting data and presentation
65	- Logic is testable as any Rust code — and full CLI invocations are testable in-process via the [`standout-test`](guides/intro-to-testing.md) harness, without subprocess spawning or stdout parsing
66	- Boilerplateless: declaratively link your handlers to command names and templates, Standout handles the rest
67	- Autodispatch: save keystrokes with auto dispatch from the known command tree
68	- Free [output handling](topics/output-modes.md): rich terminal with graceful degradation, plus structured data (JSON, YAML, CSV)
69	- Finely crafted output:
70	  - File-based [templates](crates/render/topics/templating.md) for content and CSS for styling
71	  - Rich styling with [adaptive properties](crates/render/topics/styling-system.md) (light/dark modes), inheritance, and full theming
72	  - Powerful templating through [MiniJinja](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/minijinja), including partials (reusable, smaller templates for models displayed in multiple places)
73	  - [Hot reload](crates/render/topics/file-system-resources.md): changes to templates and styles don't require compiling
74	  - Declarative layout support for [tabular data](crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md)
75	
76	## Quick Start
77	
78	### 1. Define Your Commands and Handlers
79	
80	Use the `Dispatch` derive macro to connect commands to typed handler adapters.
81	
82	```rust
83	use standout::cli::{CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
84	use standout::handler;
85	use clap::{Parser, Subcommand};
86	use serde::Serialize;
87	use todo_core::{Todo, TodoFilter, TodoStore};
88	
89	#[derive(Parser)]
90	#[command(name = "myapp")]
91	pub struct Cli {
92	    #[command(subcommand)]
93	    pub command: Commands,
94	}
95	
96	#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
97	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]  // handlers are in the `handlers` module
98	pub enum Commands {
99	    #[dispatch(pure)]
100	    List,
101	    #[dispatch(pure)]
102	    Add { title: String },
103	}
104	
105	#[derive(Serialize)]
106	struct TodoResult {
107	    todos: Vec<Todo>,
108	}
109	
110	mod handlers {
111	    use super::*;
112	
113	    #[handler]
114	    pub fn list(#[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
115	        let core = ctx.app_state.get_required::<TodoStore>()?;
116	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult { todos: core.list(TodoFilter::Pending) }))
117	    }
118	
119	    #[handler]
120	    pub fn add(
121	        #[arg] title: String,
122	        #[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext,
123	    ) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
124	        let core = ctx.app_state.get_required::<TodoStore>()?;
125	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult { todos: vec![core.add(title)?] }))
126	    }
127	}
128	```
129	
130	### 2. Define Your Presentation
131	
132	Templates use MiniJinja with semantic style tags. Styles are defined separately in CSS.
133	
134	```jinja
135	{# list.jinja #}
136	[title]My Todos[/title]
137	{% for todo in todos %}
138	  - {{ todo.title }} ([status]{{ todo.status }}[/status])
139	{% endfor %}
140	```
141	
142	```css
143	/* styles/default.css */
144	.title { color: cyan; font-weight: bold; }
145	.status { color: yellow; }
146	```
147	
148	### 3. Wire It Up
149	
150	```rust
151	use clap::CommandFactory;
152	use standout::cli::App;
153	use standout::{embed_templates, embed_styles};
154	use todo_core::TodoStore;
155	
156	fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
157	    let store = TodoStore::load("todos.json")?;
158	    let app = App::builder()
159	        .app_state(store) // the handlers above read it back with `get_required`
160	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
161	        .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
162	        .default_theme("default")
163	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())? // Register handlers from derive macro
164	        .build()?;
165	
166	    app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
167	    Ok(())
168	}
169	```
170	
171	Run it:
172	
173	```bash
174	myapp list              # Rich terminal output with colors
175	myapp list --output json    # JSON for scripting
176	myapp list --output yaml    # YAML for config files
177	myapp list --output text    # Plain text, no ANSI codes
178	```
179	
180	## Features
181	
182	### Architecture
183	
184	- CLI-free library separated from shell presentation
185	- Handlers adapt library results; framework handles rendering
186	- Core behavior and CLI adapters testable without stdout capture
187	
188	### Output Modes
189	
190	- Rich terminal output with colors and styles
191	- Automatic JSON, YAML, CSV serialization from the same handler
192	- Graceful degradation when terminal lacks capabilities
193	
194	### Rendering
195	
196	- [MiniJinja](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/minijinja) templates with semantic style tags
197	- CSS stylesheets with light/dark mode support
198	- Hot reload during development—edit templates without recompiling
199	- Tabular layouts with alignment, truncation, and Unicode support
200	
201	### Integration
202	
203	- Clap integration with automatic dispatch
204	- Declarative command registration via derive macros
205	
206	## Installation
207	
208	```bash
209	cargo add standout standout-dispatch
210	```

212	## Migrating an Existing CLI
213	
214	Already have a CLI? Standout supports incremental adoption. `run` reports
215	whether Standout handled the command:
216	
217	```rust
218	if !app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args()) {
219	    your_existing_dispatch();
220	}
221	```
222	
223	Use `run_to_string(...)` and match `DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches)` on
224	`into_outcome()` when the legacy dispatcher needs the unmatched `ArgMatches`.
225	
226	See the [Partial Adoption Guide](crates/dispatch/topics/partial-adoption.md) for the full migration path.

1	# Minimal single-crate example
2	
3	This self-contained project is a compact way to see Standout's dispatch and
4	rendering pipeline. It keeps everything in one binary package for brevity; it
5	is not the recommended layout for an application with reusable logic.
6	
7	For production-shaped ownership, continue to the
8	[two-package worked application](production-shaped-example.md), where a
9	CLI-free library owns application behavior and a binary owns all CLI concerns.
10	
11	## File structure
12	
13	```text
14	my-todo/
15	├── Cargo.toml
16	└── src/
17	    ├── main.rs
18	    ├── templates/list.jinja
19	    └── styles/default.css
20	```
21	
22	## Cargo.toml
23	
24	```toml
25	[package]
26	name = "my-todo"
27	version = "0.1.0"
28	edition = "2021"
29	
30	[dependencies]
31	standout = "9"
32	clap = { version = "4", features = ["derive"] }
33	serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
34	anyhow = "1"
35	```
36	
37	## `src/main.rs`
38	
39	```rust
40	use clap::{CommandFactory, Parser, Subcommand};
41	use serde::Serialize;
42	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
43	use standout::{embed_styles, embed_templates, handler};
44	
45	#[derive(Parser)]
46	#[command(name = "my-todo")]
47	struct Cli {
48	    #[command(subcommand)]
49	    command: Option<Commands>,
50	}
51	
52	#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
53	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
54	enum Commands {
55	    /// List all todos. Running the binary with no command lists too.
56	    #[dispatch(pure, default)]
57	    List,
58	}
59	
60	#[derive(Serialize)]
61	struct TodoResult {
62	    todos: Vec<TodoView>,
63	}
64	
65	#[derive(Serialize)]
66	struct TodoView {
67	    title: String,
68	    status: String,
69	}
70	
71	mod handlers {
72	    use super::*;
73	
74	    // This is a CLI adapter returning view data. In a real application it
75	    // should call a CLI-free library rather than contain application behavior.
76	    #[handler]
77	    pub fn list(
78	        #[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext,
79	    ) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
80	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult {
81	            todos: vec![
82	                TodoView { title: "Write documentation".into(), status: "done".into() },
83	                TodoView { title: "Ship v1.0".into(), status: "pending".into() },
84	            ],
85	        }))
86	    }
87	}
88	
89	fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
90	    let app = App::builder()
91	        .version(env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))
92	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
93	        .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
94	        .default_theme("default")
95	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
96	        .build()?;
97	
98	    app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
99	    Ok(())
100	}
101	```
102	
103	## `src/templates/list.jinja`
104	
105	```jinja
106	[title]My Todos[/title]
107	{% for todo in todos %}
108	[index]{{ loop.index }}.[/index] [{{ todo.status }}]{{ todo.title }}[/{{ todo.status }}]
109	{% endfor %}
110	```
111

113	
114	```css

116	.index { color: yellow; }
117	.done { color: gray; text-decoration: line-through; }
118	.pending { color: white; font-weight: bold; }
119	
120	@media (prefers-color-scheme: light) {
121	    .pending { color: black; }
122	}

127	```bash
128	cargo run
129	cargo run -- list
130	cargo run -- list --output json
131	cargo run -- list --output text
132	```

134	This demonstrates command dispatch, template rendering, structured output, hot
135	reload in debug builds, adaptive styles, and standout's themed `--help`, which
136	is on unless an application calls `.help_handling(false)`. It intentionally
137	does not teach package ownership or the testing pyramid; the
138	[production-shaped example](production-shaped-example.md) does.

1	# Templating
2	
3	`standout-render` uses a two-pass templating system that combines a template engine for logic and data binding with a custom BBCode-like syntax for styling. This separation keeps templates readable while providing full control over both content and presentation.
4	
5	The default engine is MiniJinja (Jinja2-compatible), but alternative engines are available. See [Template Engines](template-engines.md) for options including a lightweight `SimpleEngine` for reduced binary size.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## Two-Pass Rendering Pipeline
10	
11	Templates are processed in two distinct passes:
12	
13	```text
14	Template + Data → [Pass 1: MiniJinja] → Text with style tags → [Pass 2: BBParser] → Final output
15	```
16	
17	**Pass 1 - MiniJinja**: Standard template processing. Variables are substituted, control flow executes, filters apply.
18	
19	**Pass 2 - BBParser**: Style tag processing. Bracket-notation tags are converted to ANSI escape codes (or stripped, depending on output mode).
20	
21	### Pipeline Example
22	
23	```text
24	Template:     [title]{{ name }}[/title] has {{ count }} items
25	Data:         { name: "Report", count: 42 }
26	
27	After Pass 1: [title]Report[/title] has 42 items
28	After Pass 2: \x1b[1;36mReport\x1b[0m has 42 items  (or plain: "Report has 42 items")
29	```
30	
31	This separation means:
32	
33	- Template logic (loops, conditionals) is handled by MiniJinja—a mature, well-documented engine
34	- Style application is a simple, predictable transformation
35	- You can debug each pass independently
36	
37	---
38	
39	## MiniJinja Basics
40	
41	MiniJinja implements Jinja2 syntax, a widely-used templating language. Here's a quick overview:
42	
43	### Variables
44	
45	```jinja
46	{{ variable }}
47	{{ object.field }}
48	{{ list[0] }}
49	```
50	
51	### Control Flow
52	
53	```jinja
54	{% if condition %}
55	  Show this
56	{% elif other_condition %}
57	  Show that
58	{% else %}
59	  Default
60	{% endif %}
61	
62	{% for item in items %}
63	  {{ loop.index }}. {{ item.name }}
64	{% endfor %}
65	```
66	
67	### Filters
68	
69	```jinja
70	{{ name | upper }}
71	{{ list | length }}
72	{{ value | default("N/A") }}
73	{{ text | truncate(20) }}
74	```
75	
76	### Comments
77	
78	```jinja
79	{# This is a comment and won't appear in output #}
80	```
81	
82	For comprehensive MiniJinja documentation, see the [MiniJinja documentation](https://docs.rs/minijinja).
83	
84	### Booleans and None
85	
86	Standout renders these the Rust way — `true`, `false`, `none` — not the Jinja2
87	way MiniJinja itself uses (`True`, `False`, `None`). This holds for
88	interpolation, loop and `set` bindings, `| string`, `| join`, sequence and map
89	literals, standout's own filters, and table cells:
90	
91	```jinja
92	{{ flag }}                {# true #}
93	{{ missing }}             {# none #}
94	{{ flags }}               {# [true, false, none] #}
95	{{ flags | join(", ") }}  {# true, false, none #}
96	```
97	
98	Two exceptions:
99	
100	- The `~` concatenation operator formats inside MiniJinja's evaluator, which
101	  exposes no hook: `{{ "x" ~ flag }}` yields `xTrue`. Write `{{ "x" }}{{ flag }}`
102	  or `{{ "x" ~ flag | string }}`.
103	- Structured output (JSON, YAML, XML, CSV) skips templates entirely and
104	  serializes your data directly, so those modes follow their format's own rules.
105	
106	If you build a `minijinja::Environment` yourself, use
107	`standout_render::template::new_environment()` — or call `register_filters` on
108	your own environment, which installs the same spelling.
109	
110	---
111	
112	## The Trailing-Newline Contract
113	
114	Two things happen to the newline at the end of a template, and together they
115	are observable in the bytes a script reads, so they are stated here rather than
116	discovered by probing.
117	
118	**The engine consumes exactly one final newline.** This is Jinja's rule and
119	MiniJinja keeps it. A template file ending in a single `\n` renders with no
120	trailing newline at all; a file ending in two renders with one.
121	
122	| Template source | Rendered string |
123	| --- | --- |
124	| `{{ name }}` | `x` |
125	| `{{ name }}\n` | `x` |
126	| `{{ name }}\n\n` | `x\n` |
127	| `{{ name }}\n\n\n` | `x\n\n` |
128	
129	**The process edge appends exactly one newline.** `App::run` writes a handled
130	command's text with `writeln!`, so what reaches stdout is the rendered string
131	plus one `\n` — whatever the template ended with.
132	
133	The practical consequence: a template that ends with one newline and a template
134	that ends with none produce identical bytes. To end a page with a blank line,
135	the template needs *two* trailing newlines. Every editor that adds a final
136	newline on save is therefore invisible here, which is the reason the rule is
137	worth stating.
138	
139	`standout-render/tests/trailing_newline.rs` pins the engine half;
140	`final_emission_routes_success_and_diagnostics_to_distinct_streams` in
141	`standout/src/cli/builder/execution.rs` pins the process half.
142	
143	---
144	
145	## Style Tags
146	
147	Style tags use BBCode-like bracket notation to apply named styles from your theme:
148	
149	```jinja
150	[style-name]content to style[/style-name]
151	```
152	
153	### Basic Usage
154	
155	```jinja
156	[title]Report Summary[/title]
157	[error]Something went wrong![/error]
158	[muted]Last updated: {{ timestamp }}[/muted]
159	```
160	
161	### Nesting
162	
163	Tags can nest properly:
164	
165	```jinja
166	[outer][inner]nested content[/inner][/outer]
167	```
168	
169	### Spanning Lines
170	
171	Tags can span multiple lines:
172	
173	```jinja
174	[panel]
175	This is a multi-line
176	block of styled content
177	[/panel]
178	```
179	
180	### With Template Logic
181	
182	Style tags and MiniJinja work together seamlessly:
183	
184	```jinja
185	[title]{% if custom_title %}{{ custom_title }}{% else %}Default Title{% endif %}[/title]
186	
187	{% for task in tasks %}
188	[{{ task.status }}]{{ task.title }}[/{{ task.status }}]
189	{% endfor %}
190	```
191	
192	The second example shows dynamic style names—the style applied depends on the value of `task.status`.
193	
194	---
195	
196	## Processing Modes
197	
198	Pass 2 (BBParser) processes style tags differently based on the output mode:
199	
200	| Mode | Behavior | Use Case |
201	| ------ | ---------- | ---------- |
202	| `Term` | Replace tags with ANSI escape codes | Rich terminal output |
203	| `Text` | Strip tags completely | Plain text, pipes, files |
204	| `TermDebug` | Keep tags as literal text | Debugging, testing |
205	
206	### Processing Modes Example
207	
208	Template: `[title]Hello[/title]`
209	
210	- **Term**: `\x1b[1;36mHello\x1b[0m` (rendered as cyan bold)
211	- **Text**: `Hello`
212	- **TermDebug**: `[title]Hello[/title]`
213	
214	### Setting the Mode
215	
216	```rust
217	use standout_render::{render_with_output, OutputMode};
218	
219	// Rich terminal
220	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term)?;
221	
222	// Plain text
223	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Text)?;
224	
225	// Debug (tags visible)
226	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::TermDebug)?;
227	
228	// Auto-detect based on TTY
229	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Auto)?;
230	```
231	
232	### Auto Mode
233	
234	`OutputMode::Auto` detects the appropriate mode:
235	
236	- If stdout is a TTY with color support → `Term`
237	- If stdout is a pipe or redirect → `Text`
238	
239	> **For standout framework users:** The framework's `--output` CLI flag automatically sets the output mode. See standout documentation for details.
240	
241	---
242	
243	## Built-in Filters
244	
245	Beyond MiniJinja's standard filters, `standout-render` provides formatting filters:
246	
247	### Column Formatting
248	
249	```jinja
250	{{ value | col(10) }}                              {# pad/truncate to 10 chars #}
251	{{ value | col(20, align="right") }}               {# right-align in 20 chars #}
252	{{ value | col(15, truncate="middle") }}           {# truncate in middle #}
253	{{ value | col(15, truncate="start", ellipsis="...") }}
254	```
255	
256	### Padding
257	
258	```jinja
259	{{ "42" | pad_left(8) }}      {# "      42" #}
260	{{ "hi" | pad_right(8) }}     {# "hi      " #}
261	{{ "hi" | pad_center(8) }}    {# "   hi   " #}
262	```
263	
264	### Truncation
265	
266	```jinja
267	{{ long_text | truncate_at(20) }}                   {# "Very long text th..." #}
268	{{ path | truncate_at(30, "middle", "...") }}      {# "/home/.../file.txt" #}
269	{{ text | truncate_at(20, "start") }}              {# "...end of the text" #}
270	```
271	
272	### Display Width
273	
274	```jinja
275	{% if value | display_width > 20 %}
276	  {{ value | truncate_at(20) }}
277	{% else %}
278	  {{ value }}
279	{% endif %}
280	```
281	
282	Returns visual width (handles Unicode—CJK characters count as 2).
283	
284	### Style Application
285	
286	```jinja
287	{{ value | style_as("error") }}                    {# wraps in [error]...[/error] #}
288	{{ task.status | style_as(task.status) }}         {# dynamic: [pending]pending[/pending] #}
289	```
290	
291	---
292	
293	## Template Registry
294	
295	When using the `Renderer` struct, templates are resolved by name through a registry:
296	
297	```rust
298	use standout_render::Renderer;
299	
300	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(theme)?;
301	
302	// Add inline template
303	renderer.add_template("greeting", "Hello, [name]{{ name }}[/name]!")?;
304	
305	// Add directory of templates
306	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
307	
308	// Render by name
309	let output = renderer.render("greeting", &data)?;
310	```
311	
312	### Resolution Priority
313	
314	1. **Inline templates** (added via `add_template()`)
315	2. **Directory templates** (from `add_template_dir()`)
316	
317	### File Extensions
318	
319	Supported extensions (in priority order): `.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`, `.stpl`, `.txt`
320	
321	When you request `"report"`, the registry checks:
322	
323	- Inline template named `"report"`
324	- `report.jinja` in registered directories
325	- `report.jinja2`, `report.j2`, `report.stpl`, `report.txt` (lower priority)
326	
327	The `.stpl` extension is for SimpleEngine templates. See [Template Engines](template-engines.md) for details.
328	
329	### Template Names
330	
331	Template names are derived from relative paths:
332	
333	```text
334	templates/
335	├── greeting.jinja       → "greeting"
336	├── reports/
337	│   └── summary.jinja    → "reports/summary"
338	└── errors/
339	    └── 404.jinja        → "errors/404"
340	```
341	
342	---
343	
344	## Including Templates
345	
346	Templates can include other templates using MiniJinja's include syntax:
347	
348	```jinja
349	{# main.jinja #}
350	[title]{{ title }}[/title]
351	
352	{% include "partials/header.jinja" %}
353	
354	{% for item in items %}
355	  {% include "partials/item.jinja" %}
356	{% endfor %}
357	
358	{% include "partials/footer.jinja" %}
359	```
360	
361	This enables reusable components across your application.
362	
363	---
364	
365	## Context Variables
366	
367	Beyond your data, you can inject additional context into templates:
368	
369	```rust
370	use standout_render::{render_with_vars, OutputMode};
371	use std::collections::HashMap;
372	
373	let mut vars = HashMap::new();
374	vars.insert("version", "1.0.0");
375	vars.insert("app_name", "MyApp");
376	
377	let output = render_with_vars(
378	    "{{ app_name }} v{{ version }}: {{ message }}",
379	    &data,
380	    &theme,
381	    OutputMode::Term,
382	    vars,
383	)?;
384	```
385	
386	When handler data and context variables have the same key, **handler data wins**. Context is supplementary.
387	
388	---
389	
390	## Structured Output
391	
392	For machine-readable output (JSON, YAML, CSV), templates are bypassed entirely:
393	
394	```rust
395	use standout_render::{render_auto, OutputMode};
396	
397	// Template is used for Term/Text modes
398	// Data is serialized directly for Json/Yaml/Csv
399	let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
400	```
401	
402	| Mode | Behavior |
403	| ------ | ---------- |
404	| `Term` | Render template, apply styles |
405	| `Text` | Render template, strip styles |
406	| `TermDebug` | Render template, keep style tags |
407	| `Json` | `serde_json::to_string_pretty(data)` |
408	| `Yaml` | `serde_yaml::to_string(data)` |
409	| `Csv` | Flatten and format as CSV |
410	
411	This means your serializable data types automatically support structured output without additional code.
412	
413	---
414	
415	## Validation
416	
417	Check templates for unknown style tags before deploying:
418	
419	```rust
420	use standout_render::validate_template;
421	
422	let errors = validate_template(template, &sample_data, &theme);
423	if !errors.is_empty() {
424	    for error in &errors {
425	        eprintln!("Unknown style tag: [{}]", error.tag_name);
426	    }
427	}
428	```
429	
430	Validation catches:
431	
432	- Misspelled style names
433	- References to undefined styles
434	- Mismatched opening/closing tags
435

437	
438	## API Reference
439	
440	### Render Functions
441	
442	```rust
443	use standout_render::{
444	    render,                  // Basic: template + data + theme
445	    render_with_output,      // With explicit output mode
446	    render_with_mode,        // With output mode + color mode
447	    render_with_vars,        // With extra context variables
448	    render_auto,             // Auto-dispatch template vs serialize
449	    render_auto_with_context,
450	};
451	
452	// Basic
453	let output = render(template, &data, &theme)?;
454	
455	// With output mode
456	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term)?;
457	
458	// With color mode override (for testing)
459	let output = render_with_mode(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term, ColorMode::Dark)?;
460	
461	// Auto (template for text modes, serialize for structured)
462	let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
463	```
464	
465	### Renderer Struct
466	
467	```rust
468	use standout_render::Renderer;
469	
470	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(theme)?;
471	renderer.add_template("name", "content")?;
472	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
473	
474	let output = renderer.render("name", &data)?;
475	let output = renderer.render_with_mode("name", &data, OutputMode::Text)?;
476	```

1	# Styled Help
2	
3	Standout can replace clap's built-in help with themed, template-driven output. Instead of clap's fixed format, your `--help` renders through the same MiniJinja + style-tag pipeline as the rest of your CLI.
4	
5	This gives you bold headers, consistent alignment, and a "Learn More" section linking to help topics. For CLIs with many commands, you can organize subcommands into named groups with section headers, help text, and visual separators.
6	
7	## Help Handling
8	
9	Help interception is **on by default**. An app that configures nothing renders
10	themed help; `.help_handling(false)` gives clap's own help back:
11	
12	```rust
13	// Themed help, no call needed.
14	App::builder().build()?;
15	
16	// Clap's own help instead.
17	App::builder().help_handling(false).build()?;
18	```
19	
20	With help handling on, standout:
21	
22	1. Disables clap's default `help` subcommand and registers its own (with `--page` for pager support), subject to the [install policy](#the-help-word) below
23	2. **Keeps** clap's native `--help`/`-h` flag, on purpose: clap's flag short-circuits argument validation, so `myapp build --help` renders even when required arguments are missing
24	3. Intercepts all help requests and renders them through a MiniJinja template with style tags — the `help` word, which clap routes like any other subcommand, and clap's `DisplayHelp` (from `--help`/`-h`, at root and subcommand level)
25	
26	Every form that is available renders the same help, through the same template and theme — with one exception, which is about the *form*, not the entry point: `--output` reaches the `help` word but not the flags. `myapp help --output text` renders in text mode; `myapp --help --output text` renders in `Auto` and the mode is ignored. The reason is where each form is answered: the word is a subcommand, so clap parses its line in full, globals included, while `--help` short-circuits inside clap before the parse completes — so there are no matches to read a mode from when its `DisplayHelp` is rendered.
27	
28	Subcommand-level help (e.g. `myapp build --help`) also works, rendering that subcommand's help through standout.
29	
30	**Incompatible with the opt-out:** `command_groups` and topics need help interception to render. Configuring either alongside `.help_handling(false)` returns a `SetupError` from `build()`.
31	
32	### Whichever entry point you use
33	
34	Help is answered the same way through both parse paths — `run()` / `run_with()` and `get_matches_from()`. Same install policy for the word, same interception of `--help` / `-h`, same rendering: an application's entry point is not a fact about what `myapp help` means.
35	
36	The one thing the two paths cannot share is `--page`, because paging is a terminal side effect and only a *printing* entry point may perform it. `run()` hands the text to the pager; the capture APIs return it instead — `run_with()` marks it `SuccessKind::PagedHelp`, `get_matches_from()` returns `HelpResult::PagedHelp` — and leave the decision to you.
37	
38	## The `help` Word
39	
40	`--help` and `-h` are flags: they are always available and can never collide with your data. A bare `help` is different — at the root of a CLI with no subcommands, a bare word is *data*. `echo help`, `grep help`, and `ls help` all treat it as such, and a tool whose positional is a revision range or a file name would be wrong to swallow it.
41	
42	So standout only installs the word where it knows nothing else can claim it:
43	
44	| Root shape | `help` word |
45	| --- | --- |
46	| Has subcommands | Installed — a bare word there is already a command |
47	| Flat, no positionals | Installed — nothing to collide with |
48	| Flat, with positionals | **Opt-in only** — see below |
49	
50	For the third shape, only your application knows whether its positional domain excludes the word. Opt in with `.help_word(true)`:
51	
52	```rust
53	// `mytool <RANGE>` — a revision range is never the word "help".
54	App::builder().help_word(true).build()?;
55	```
56	
57	Opting in accepts the cost: the literal word `help` can no longer reach the positional, and `--` becomes the escape for it — `mytool -- help` passes the string through. Without the opt-in, `--help` / `-h` remain the only spelling, and they still render themed help.
58	
59	`help_word(true)` only ever *adds* the word; it is not a way to suppress `help` on a CLI that has subcommands. It cannot be combined with `.help_handling(false)` — the word is standout's own subcommand, so `build()` returns a `SetupError` without interception.
60	
61	### On a flat CLI, the word describes a flat CLI
62	
63	Clap's `help` is worded for a CLI with subcommands — "Print this message or the
64	help of the given subcommand(s)". On a flat CLI that sentence points at a
65	namespace that cannot exist, and the flat shape is exactly the one
66	`help_word(true)` serves. So the word describes the shape it is installed on:
67	
68	| Root shape | `help` about |
69	| --- | --- |
70	| Has subcommands | Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s) |
71	| Flat | Print this message |
72	
73	A flat CLI also drops the COMMANDS section entirely when `help` would be its
74	only entry. The word is machinery standout installs, not part of your surface,
75	and a section listing nothing but the command that printed it is noise:
76	
77	```text
78	COMMANDS
79	  help          Print this message
80	```
81	
82	Registered topics earn the section back, because `help <topic>` is then a real
83	destination and the word is how a reader reaches it. A root with commands of its
84	own always keeps its section, `help` included.
85	
86	### If your CLI already has a `help`
87	
88	Where standout installs the word, the name is standout's. An application that claims it too — a clap subcommand called `help` (or aliased to it), or a registration whose first path segment is `help` (`.command_with("help", …)`, `.command_with("help.topic", …)`, a `.commands(|g| g.group("help", …))`) — is a configuration standout refuses rather than serves:
89	
90	```text
91	duplicate command: help — this application's clap `Command` declares `help` (as a
92	subcommand name or alias), and standout installs a `help` word of its own, since
93	help handling is on by default. Rename the application's command, or call
94	.help_handling(false) to keep the name (help is then clap's own, and
95	command_groups and topics become unavailable)
96	```
97	
98	Each spelling is caught the moment it becomes visible: a registration under the root `help` fails `build()`, while a clap-declared one is only visible when your `Command` reaches a parse entry point, so it comes back as `HelpResult::Error` / `DispatchResult::Error` before anything is parsed. Neither reaches clap, whose answer to two subcommands of one name is a debug assertion — a panic on a configuration, which is what `SetupError` exists to prevent.
99	
100	Standing down — letting your `help` win and rendering nothing itself — is deliberately not offered. `myapp help` would then run your handler while `myapp --help` rendered standout's themed help: one CLI answering the same question two ways.
101	
102	Unaffected: a `help` deeper in the tree (`myapp db help` is yours, at a path the word is never installed on), and any root that never gets the word — a flat CLI with positionals and no `.help_word(true)`, or any CLI built with `.help_handling(false)`.
103	
104	### Why the word is reachable at all
105	
106	On a flat CLI whose root arguments are required, an injected `help` subcommand used to be advertised in help output and impossible to run: clap validates the root's requirements before routing, so `myapp help` failed with "the following required arguments were not provided" instead of printing help.
107	
108	The fix is a declaration, not a parser of standout's own. Where standout installs the word, it also sets clap's `subcommand_negates_reqs`, which suspends the root's requirements once a command is named — so `myapp help` routes to the word, while `myapp` on its own still reports its missing arguments and `myapp <RANGE>` still parses as data. The word's arguments (`myapp help topics`, `myapp help --page`, `myapp help --output text`) are clap's to parse, like any other subcommand's.
109	
110	The cost is worth naming: `subcommand_negates_reqs` applies to *your* subcommands too, so a root that declares required arguments stops requiring them once any command is named. That is why standout sets it only where it installs the word, and never on a CLI that did not get one. See [ADR-0018](../adr/0018-let-the-parser-classify-the-command-line.md).
111	
112	## Short and Long Help
113	
114	Clap gives a command a terse `about` and an optional full `long_about`, and its
115	convention is that `-h` shows the first while `--help` shows the second. Themed
116	help keeps that distinction:
117	
118	| Invocation | Renders |
119	| --- | --- |
120	| `-h` | `about` |
121	| `--help` | `long_about`, falling back to `about` |
122	| `help` | `long_about`, falling back to `about` — the spelled-out request reads like `--help` |
123	
124	Standout has to recover the spelling itself: `--help` short-circuits inside clap
125	and arrives as a `DisplayHelp` error that names neither the flag that raised it
126	nor the command it was raised for. Both are recovered from a *parse*, not from a
127	scan of the argument list — the two flags are re-declared as ordinary global
128	arguments on a throwaway clone whose own help flag is disabled, and clap
129	answers. That keeps `--` termination, `--flag=value`, short-option clusters, and
130	option-value consumption (`-o h` is not a help request) the parser's business,
131	per [ADR-0018](../adr/0018-let-the-parser-classify-the-command-line.md).
132	
133	Rendering help yourself with [`render_help`](#standalone-rendering) has no
134	invocation to classify, so it defaults to `HelpLength::Short`. Ask for the full
135	text with `length`:
136	
137	```rust
138	let config = HelpConfig {
139	    length: HelpLength::Long,
140	    ..Default::default()
141	};
142	```
143	
144	## What an Option Row Shows
145	
146	Option rows carry the information clap surfaces about an argument — its
147	value syntax, description, default, and accepted values:
148	
149	```text
150	OPTIONS
151	  --staged            Diff the staged changes
152	  --threshold <RATIO> Move/rename similarity threshold
153	  -c, --color <BOOL>  Enable ANSI color
154	  --output            Output format
155	                      default: auto
156	                      possible values: auto, term, text, term-debug, json, yaml, xml, csv
157	  --output-file-path  Write output to file instead of stdout
158	```
159	
160	The default and possible-value lines hang under the description column and
161	carry their own `[default]` and `[values]` tags, so a stylesheet can dim or
162	recolor them independently. Standout writes them as words rather than clap's
163	`[default: auto]` brackets: literal `[` would have to be escaped through the
164	style-tag parser, and the emphasis belongs to the theme. Hidden possible values
165	(`PossibleValue::hide`) are left out.
166	
167	Options that take values render their metavar alongside the spelling, using an
168	explicit `value_name` when present and clap's fallback display otherwise. Pure
169	presence flags such as `ArgAction::SetTrue` and `SetFalse` do not render a
170	metavar and do not show parser-derived `true, false` values, because those words
171	are not valid command-line values for the flag.
172	
173	### Positionals get their own section
174	
175	Positionals render in an ARGUMENTS section ahead of OPTIONS, the way clap orders
176	them, rather than filed among the flags:
177	
178	```text
179	ARGUMENTS
180	  RANGE         Git range to diff, e.g. main..HEAD
181	
182	OPTIONS
183	  --staged      Diff the staged changes
184	```
185	
186	A positional is listed under its `value_name` when it declares one, else its
187	argument id, and is tagged `[metavar]`. The two sections size their columns
188	independently, so a long flag name does not push the ARGUMENTS column out with
189	it.
190	
191	## Styling User-Provided Strings
192	
193	When help interception is enabled, your clap `about` and `help` strings are rendered through standout's BBCode parser, so they can use any tag defined in your stylesheet:
194	
195	```rust
196	#[command(name = "myapp", about = "[bold]myapp[/bold] — a small CLI")]
197	struct Cli { /* ... */ }
198	```
199	
200	To emit a literal `[` or `]` in help text, escape it with a backslash: `\[` and `\]`. Other backslashes (file paths, regex examples like `\d+`) pass through unchanged. To emit a literal `\[`, write `\\[`.
201	
202	```rust
203	#[command(about = "Match pattern \\[regex: \\d+\\]")]
204	// renders as: Match pattern [regex: \d+]
205	```
206	
207	## Default Behavior
208	
209	Without any group configuration, all subcommands appear in a single "Commands" section:
210	
211	```text
212	My application
213	
214	USAGE
215	  myapp <COMMAND>
216	
217	COMMANDS
218	  init          Initialize the project
219	  list          List all items
220	  delete        Delete an item
221	  config        Manage configuration
222	
223	OPTIONS
224	  --output      Output format
225	                default: auto
226	                possible values: auto, term, text, term-debug, json, yaml, xml, csv
227	```
228	
229	## Command Groups
230	
231	CLIs with many commands (20+) benefit from organized help. The `CommandGroup` struct lets you split subcommands into named sections:
232	
233	```rust
234	use standout::cli::{App, CommandGroup};
235	
236	App::builder()
237	    .command_groups(vec![
238	        CommandGroup {
239	            title: "Commands".into(),
240	            help: None,
241	            commands: vec![
242	                Some("init".into()),
243	                Some("create".into()),
244	                Some("list".into()),
245	                Some("search".into()),
246	            ],
247	        },
248	        CommandGroup {
249	            title: "Per Pad(s)".into(),
250	            help: Some(
251	                "These commands accept one or more pad ids: <id> or ranges <id>-<id>\n\
252	                 ex: $ padz view 3 5 7-9  # views pads 3, 5, 7, 8 and 9".into()
253	            ),
254	            commands: vec![
255	                Some("open".into()), Some("view".into()), Some("peek".into()),
256	                None, // blank line separator
257	                Some("pin".into()), Some("unpin".into()),
258	                None,
259	                Some("complete".into()), Some("reopen".into()),
260	            ],
261	        },
262	        CommandGroup {
263	            title: "Misc".into(),
264	            help: None,
265	            commands: vec![
266	                Some("completions".into()),
267	                Some("help".into()),
268	                Some("config".into()),
269	            ],
270	        },
271	    ])
272	    .build()?;
273	```
274	
275	This produces:
276	
277	```text
278	COMMANDS
279	  init          Initialize the store
280	  create        Create a new pad
281	  list          List pads
282	  search        Search pads
283	
284	PER PAD(S)
285	  These commands accept one or more pad ids: <id> or ranges <id>-<id>
286	  ex: $ padz view 3 5 7-9  # views pads 3, 5, 7, 8 and 9
287	
288	  open          Open a pad in the editor
289	  view          View one or more pads
290	  peek          Peek at pad content previews
291	
292	  pin           Pin one or more pads
293	  unpin         Unpin one or more pads
294	
295	  complete      Mark pads as done
296	  reopen        Reopen pads
297	
298	MISC
299	  completions   Generate shell completions
300	  help          Print this message
301	  config        Get or set configuration
302	```
303	
304	### Blank Line Separators
305	
306	Use `None` entries in the `commands` vec to insert blank lines within a group. This creates visual sub-clusters without introducing nested group hierarchy:
307	
308	```rust
309	commands: vec![
310	    Some("open".into()),
311	    Some("view".into()),
312	    None,               // blank line
313	    Some("pin".into()),
314	    Some("unpin".into()),
315	],
316	```
317	
318	### Ungrouped Commands
319	
320	Commands that exist in your clap definition but don't appear in any `CommandGroup` are automatically appended to an "Other" section. This is a safety net: if you add a new subcommand but forget to add it to the group config, it still shows up in help. Silently hiding commands would be worse than slightly messy help.
321	
322	### Group Help Text
323	
324	Each group can include optional help text displayed between the section header and the command list. Use this to explain shared arguments, conventions, or usage patterns that apply to all commands in the group.
325	
326	## Standalone Rendering
327	
328	You can render help without `App` using `render_help` directly:
329	
330	```rust
331	use standout::cli::{render_help, CommandGroup, HelpConfig};
332	use standout::OutputMode;
333	
334	let config = HelpConfig {
335	    output_mode: Some(OutputMode::Text),
336	    command_groups: Some(vec![
337	        CommandGroup {
338	            title: "Main".into(),
339	            help: None,
340	            commands: vec![Some("init".into()), Some("list".into())],
341	        },
342	    ]),
343	    ..Default::default()
344	};
345	
346	let output = render_help(&cmd, Some(config))?;
347	println!("{}", output);
348	```
349	
350	## Validation
351	
352	The group config is static — it should be validated at test time, not when a user runs `--help`. Use `validate_command_groups` in a `#[test]`:
353	
354	```rust
355	use standout::cli::{validate_command_groups, CommandGroup};
356	use clap::CommandFactory;
357	
358	#[test]
359	fn test_help_groups_match_commands() {
360	    let cmd = Cli::command();
361	    let groups = my_command_groups();
362	    validate_command_groups(&cmd, &groups).unwrap();
363	}
364	```
365	
366	**What it checks:**
367	
368	- **Phantom reference** — a group names a command that doesn't exist in the clap definition (catches typos and stale configs)
369	
370	**What it allows:**
371	
372	- **Ungrouped commands** — commands not in any group are OK; they auto-append to "Other" at render time
373	
374	This follows the same pattern as `app.verify_command(&cmd)` for handler/argument validation.
375	
376	## Themes
377	
378	Help rendering uses a theme to style output. The default theme applies bold to headers and command names:
379	
380	```rust
381	pub fn default_help_theme() -> Theme {
382	    Theme::new()
383	        .add("header", Style::new().bold())   // COMMANDS, OPTIONS, etc.
384	        .add("item", Style::new().bold())     // Command/option names
385	        .add("metavar", Style::new().bold())  // Argument names in ARGUMENTS
386	        .add("desc", Style::new())            // Descriptions
387	        .add("default", Style::new().dim())   // "default: auto"
388	        .add("values", Style::new().dim())    // "possible values: ..."
389	        .add("usage", Style::new())           // Usage line
390	        .add("example", Style::new())         // Examples section
391	        .add("about", Style::new())           // About text
392	}
393	```
394	
395	A configured theme *overlays* this default rather than replacing it: per style name, an entry the configured theme defines wins, and every tag it leaves out keeps its default styling. Restyle only what you mean to change:
396	
397	```rust
398	let config = HelpConfig {
399	    theme: Some(
400	        Theme::new()
401	            .add("header", Style::new().bold().cyan())
402	            .add("item", Style::new().green())
403	    ),
404	    ..Default::default()
405	};
406	```
407	
408	Or when using `AppBuilder`, set the theme with `.theme()` — it applies to both help and command output. Because of the overlay, an application theme does not need to define the help vocabulary at all: a theme that only declares the app's own output styles leaves help rendered entirely by the default help theme.
409	
410	## Custom Templates
411	
412	The default template renders about, usage, grouped commands, options, examples, and learn-more topics. Override it via `HelpConfig::template`:
413	
414	```rust
415	let config = HelpConfig {
416	    template: Some(my_custom_template.into()),
417	    ..Default::default()
418	};
419	```
420	
421	### Template Variables
422	
423	The template receives a `HelpData` struct with these fields:
424	
425	| Variable | Type | Description |
426	| ---------- | ------ | ------------- |
427	| `about` | String | The command's `about`, or its `long_about` — see [Short and long help](#short-and-long-help) |
428	| `usage` | String | Usage line (without "Usage: " prefix) |
429	| `subcommands` | Vec | Command groups (each with `title`, `help`, `items`) |
430	| `subcommands_width` | usize | Width of the COMMANDS name column |
431	| `arguments` | Vec | Positional groups (each with `title`, `help`, `items`) |
432	| `arguments_width` | usize | Width of the ARGUMENTS name column |
433	| `options` | Vec | Flag groups (each with `title`, `help`, `items`) |
434	| `options_width` | usize | Width of the OPTIONS name column |
435	| `examples` | String | Examples text |
436	| `learn_more` | Vec | Topic list items (each with `name`, `title`) |
437	| `learn_more_width` | usize | Width of the LEARN MORE name column |
438	
439	#### Alignment is the template's job
440	
441	There are no `padding` fields. A row aligns itself by padding its name to its
442	section's width with `pad_right`, one of [standout-render's tabular
443	filters](../crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md):
444	
445	```jinja
446	{%- set opt_label = "[item]" ~ opt.name ~ "[/item]" -%}
447	{%- if opt.value_name %}
448	{%- set opt_label = opt_label ~ " [metavar]" ~ opt.value_name ~ "[/metavar]" -%}
449	{%- endif %}
450	{{ opt_label | pad_right(options_width) }}  [desc]{{ opt.help }}[/desc]
451	```
452	
453	Two properties of that filter are the point of doing it this way. It measures
454	*display* width, so a CJK name counts the terminal columns it really occupies
455	and the style tags around it count for nothing — byte length gets both wrong.
456	And it never truncates: a name wider than the column keeps its full text and
457	its separator, which is the failure the fixed-width column used to produce.
458	
459	The widths themselves are resolved from the data, as a `Width::Bounded` column
460	that is at least 12 columns wide and otherwise as wide as the section's longest
461	name. One width per *section*, not per group, is what keeps a grouped command
462	list aligned down the whole page instead of realigning at each header.
463	
464	### Group Fields in Templates
465	
466	Each subcommand group has:
467	
468	- `group.title` — section header (rendered as `group.title | upper` in the default template)
469	- `group.help` — optional help text for the group
470	- `group.items` — list of command entries
471	
472	Each command entry has:
473	
474	- `cmd.name` — command name
475	- `cmd.about` — command description
476	- `cmd.separator` — true for blank-line separator entries
477	
478	Each argument and option entry has:
479	
480	- `opt.name` — `range` / `RANGE` for a positional, `-o, --output` for a flag
481	- `opt.value_name` — rendered value syntax for a value-taking flag, such as `<MODE>` or `[<PATH>]`; empty for positionals and presence flags
482	- `opt.help` — description
483	- `opt.short` / `opt.long` — the flag's spellings (both empty for a positional)
484	- `opt.default` — the declared default, or nothing
485	- `opt.possible_values` — the selectable values, hidden ones left out
486	
487	### Example Custom Template
488	
489	```jinja
490	[about]{{ about }}[/about]
491	
492	[header]USAGE[/header]
493	  [usage]{{ usage }}[/usage]
494	{%- for group in subcommands %}
495	
496	[header]{{ group.title | upper }}[/header]
497	{%- if group.help %}
498	  [desc]{{ group.help }}[/desc]
499	{% endif %}
500	{%- for cmd in group.items %}
501	{%- if cmd.separator %}
502	
503	{%- else %}
504	  {{ ("[item]" ~ cmd.name ~ "[/item]") | pad_right(subcommands_width) }}  [desc]{{ cmd.about }}[/desc]
505	{%- endif %}
506	{%- endfor %}
507	{%- endfor %}
508	```
509	
510	Style tags like `[header]...[/header]` are resolved against the theme. Unknown tags pass through or show a `?` indicator depending on the output mode.
511	
512	## Output Modes
513	
514	The `help` word respects the `--output` flag, but only as far as *styling*. Help is always the rendered template; the mode decides what happens to its style tags — applied in `Term`, stripped in `Text`, left visible as `[header]…[/header]` in `TermDebug`:
515	
516	```bash
517	myapp help --output text
518	```
519	
520	`--help` / `-h` do not take the flag with them (see [above](#help-handling)): they render in `Auto`, which styles for the terminal it finds. Spell the mode with the word when you need it.
521	
522	The structured modes (`json`, `yaml`, `xml`, `csv`) strip the tags exactly as `Text` does. None of them serializes `HelpData`, so help is themed prose in every mode, not a machine-readable document. If you need help as data, render it yourself: `HelpData` is what a [custom template](#custom-templates) receives, and a template that emits JSON is the seam for it.
523
