1	# Execution Model
2	
3	`standout-dispatch` manages a strict linear pipeline from CLI input to rendered
4	output. This explicitly separated flow keeps handler adapters decoupled from
5	presentation (renderers) and shell pipeline side effects (hooks).
6	
7	---
8	
9	## The Pipeline
10	
11	```text
12	Clap Parsing → Pre-dispatch → Handler → Post-dispatch → Renderer → Post-output → Piping → Output
13	```
14	
15	Each stage has a clear responsibility:
16	
17	**Clap Parsing**: Your `clap::Command` definition is parsed normally. `standout-dispatch` doesn't replace clap—it works with the resulting `ArgMatches`.
18	
19	**Pre-dispatch Hook**: Runs before the handler. Can abort execution (e.g., auth checks).
20	
21	**Handler**: Your CLI adapter executes. It receives `ArgMatches` and
22	`CommandContext`, calls the CLI-free application library, and returns a
23	`HandlerResult<T>`—either data to render, a silent marker, or binary content.
24	For simpler adapters, use the `#[handler]` macro to write typed functions that
25	return `Result<T, E>` directly (see [Handler Contract](handler-contract.md)).
26	
27	**Post-dispatch Hook**: Runs after the handler, before rendering. Can transform data.
28	
29	**Renderer**: Your render function receives the data and produces output (string or binary).
30	
31	**Post-output Hook**: Runs after rendering. Can transform the final output string.
32	
33	**Piping**: Optionally sends output to external commands (jq, tee, clipboard). Implemented as specialized post-output hooks. See [Output Piping](../../pipe/topics/piping.md).
34	
35	**Output**: The result is returned or written to stdout.
36	
37	---
38	
39	## Command Paths
40	
41	A command path is a vector of strings representing the subcommand chain:
42	
43	```bash
44	myapp db migrate --steps 5
45	```
46	
47	The command path is `["db", "migrate"]`.
48	
49	### Extracting Command Paths
50	
51	```rust
52	use standout_dispatch::{extract_command_path, path_to_string, get_deepest_matches};
53	
54	let matches = cmd.get_matches();
55	
56	// Get the full path
57	let path = extract_command_path(&matches);  // ["db", "migrate"]
58	
59	// Convert to dot notation
60	let path_str = path_to_string(&path);  // "db.migrate"
61	
62	// Get ArgMatches for the deepest command
63	let deep = get_deepest_matches(&matches);  // ArgMatches for "migrate"
64	```
65	
66	### Command Path Utilities
67	
68	| Function | Purpose |
69	| ---------- | --------- |
70	| `extract_command_path` | Get subcommand chain as `Vec<String>` |
71	| `path_to_string` | Convert path to dot notation (`"db.migrate"`) |
72	| `string_to_path` | Convert dot notation to path |
73	| `get_deepest_matches` | Get `ArgMatches` for deepest subcommand |
74	| `has_subcommand` | Check if any subcommand was invoked |
75	
76	---
77	
78	## State Injection
79	
80	Handlers access state through `CommandContext`, which provides two mechanisms:
81	
82	- **`app_state`**: Shared, immutable state configured at build time (database, config)
83	- **`extensions`**: Per-request, mutable state injected by hooks
84	
85	```rust
86	fn handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T> {
87	    // App state: shared resources
88	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
89	
90	    // Extensions: per-request state
91	    let scope = ctx.extensions.get_required::<UserScope>()?;
92	    // ...
93	}
94	```
95	
96	> For full details on state management, see [App State and Extensions](app-state.md).
97	
98	---
99	
100	## The Hooks System
101	
102	Hooks are functions that run at specific points in the pipeline. They let you intercept, validate, or transform without touching handler logic—keeping concerns separated.
103	
104	### Three Phases
105	
106	**Pre-dispatch**: Runs before the handler. Can abort execution or inject per-request state.
107	
108	Use for: authentication checks, input validation, logging start time, **injecting per-request state** via `extensions`.
109	
110	Pre-dispatch hooks receive `&mut CommandContext`, allowing them to inject state via `ctx.extensions` that handlers can retrieve. They also have read access to `ctx.app_state` for shared resources:
111	
112	```rust
113	use standout_dispatch::{Hooks, HookError};
114	
115	// Per-request state types (injected by hooks)
116	struct UserSession { user_id: u64 }
117	
118	Hooks::new()
119	    .pre_dispatch(|matches, ctx| {
120	        // Read from app_state (shared)
121	        let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
122	
123	        // Validate and set up per-request state
124	        let token = std::env::var("API_TOKEN")
125	            .map_err(|_| HookError::pre_dispatch("API_TOKEN required"))?;
126	
127	        let user_id = db.validate_token(&token)?;
128	
129	        // Inject into extensions (per-request)
130	        ctx.extensions.insert(UserSession { user_id });
131	        Ok(())
132	    })
133	```
134	
135	Handlers then use both app_state and extensions:
136	
137	```rust
138	fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
139	    // App state: shared across all requests
140	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
141	
142	    // Extensions: per-request state from hooks
143	    let session = ctx.extensions.get_required::<UserSession>()?;
144	
145	    let items = db.fetch_items(session.user_id)?;
146	    Ok(Output::Render(items))
147	}
148	```
149	
150	See [App State and Extensions](app-state.md#extensions-per-request-state) for the `Extensions` API and the two-state model.
151	
152	**Post-dispatch**: Runs after the handler, before rendering. Can transform data.
153	
154	Use for: adding timestamps, filtering sensitive fields, data enrichment. The hook receives handler output as `serde_json::Value`, allowing generic transformations regardless of the handler's output type.
155	
156	```rust
157	Hooks::new().post_dispatch(|_matches, _ctx, mut data| {
158	    if let Some(obj) = data.as_object_mut() {
159	        obj.insert("generated_at".into(), json!(Utc::now().to_rfc3339()));
160	    }
161	    Ok(data)
162	})
163	```
164	
165	**Post-output**: Runs after rendering. Can transform the final string.
166	
167	Use for: adding headers/footers, logging, metrics. The hook receives `RenderedOutput`—an enum of `Text(TextOutput)`, `Binary(Vec<u8>, String)`, `Artifact(ArtifactOutput)`, or `Silent`. For an artifact the bytes and report are still pre-write, so a hook may transform them via `as_artifact_mut()`; the framework, not the hook, performs the final write.
168	
169	```rust
170	use standout_dispatch::RenderedOutput;
171	
172	Hooks::new().post_output(|_matches, _ctx, output| {
173	    match output {
174	        RenderedOutput::Text(s) => {
175	            Ok(RenderedOutput::Text(format!("{}\n-- Generated by MyApp", s)))
176	        }
177	        other => Ok(other),
178	    }
179	})
180	```
181	
182	### Hook Chaining
183	
184	Multiple hooks per phase are supported. Pre-dispatch hooks run sequentially—first error aborts. Post-dispatch and post-output hooks *chain*: each receives the output of the previous, enabling composable transformations.
185	
186	```rust
187	Hooks::new()
188	    .post_dispatch(add_metadata)      // Runs first
189	    .post_dispatch(filter_sensitive)  // Receives add_metadata's output
190	```
191	
192	Order matters: `filter_sensitive` sees the metadata that `add_metadata` inserted.
193	
194	### Output Piping
195	
196	Piping sends rendered output to external shell commands. It's implemented as specialized post-output hooks with three modes:
197	
198	```rust
199	use standout::cli::App;
200	
201	let app = App::builder()
202	    .commands(|g| {
203	        g.command_with("export", handlers::export, |cfg| {
204	            cfg.template_name("export")
205	               // Filter through jq (capture mode)
206	               .pipe_through("jq '.items'")
207	        })
208	        .command_with("copy", handlers::copy, |cfg| {
209	            cfg.template_name("copy")
210	               // Send to clipboard (consume mode)
211	               .pipe_to_clipboard()
212	        })
213	        .command_with("debug", handlers::debug, |cfg| {
214	            cfg.template_name("debug")
215	               // Log to file while displaying (passthrough mode)
216	               .pipe_to("tee /tmp/debug.log")
217	        })
218	    })
219	    .build()?;
220	```
221	
222	| Mode | Method | Behavior |
223	| ------ | -------- | ---------- |
224	| Passthrough | `pipe_to()` | Run command, return original output |
225	| Capture | `pipe_through()` | Return command's stdout as new output |
226	| Consume | `pipe_to_clipboard()` | Send to clipboard, return empty |
227	
228	Pipes can be chained and combined with other post-output hooks. See [Output Piping](../../pipe/topics/piping.md) for full documentation.
229	
230	### Error Handling
231	
232	When a hook returns `Err(HookError)`:
233	
234	- Execution stops immediately
235	- Remaining hooks in that phase don't run
236	- For pre-dispatch: the handler never executes
237	- For post phases: the rendered output is discarded
238	- The error message is returned
239	
240	```rust
241	use standout_dispatch::HookError;
242	
243	// Create error with phase context
244	HookError::pre_dispatch("database connection failed")
245	
246	// With source error for debugging
247	HookError::post_dispatch("transformation failed")
248	    .with_source(underlying_error)
249	```
250	
251	---
252	
253	## Default Command Support
254	
255	Handle the case when no subcommand is specified:
256	
257	```rust
258	use standout_dispatch::{has_subcommand, insert_default_command};
259	
260	let matches = cmd.get_matches_from(args);
261	
262	if !has_subcommand(&matches) {
263	    // Re-parse with default command inserted
264	    let args_with_default = insert_default_command(std::env::args(), "list");
265	    let matches = cmd.get_matches_from(args_with_default);
266	    // Now dispatch to "list"
267	}
268	```
269	
270	`insert_default_command` inserts the command name after the binary name but before any flags.
271	
272	---
273	
274	## Putting It Together
275	
276	A complete dispatch flow:
277	
278	```rust
279	use standout_dispatch::{
280	    SimpleFnHandler, FnHandler, Output, CommandContext, Hooks, HookError,
281	    extract_command_path, get_deepest_matches, path_to_string,
282	};
283	
284	fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
285	    // 1. Define clap command
286	    let cmd = Command::new("myapp")
287	        .subcommand(Command::new("list"))
288	        .subcommand(Command::new("delete").arg(Arg::new("id").required(true)));
289	
290	    // 2. Create handlers
291	    // SimpleFnHandler: for handlers that don't need CommandContext
292	    let list_handler = SimpleFnHandler::new(|_m| {
293	        storage::list()  // Result<T, E> auto-wraps in Output::Render
294	    });
295	
296	    // FnHandler: when you need CommandContext
297	    let delete_handler = FnHandler::new(|matches, _ctx| {
298	        let id: &String = matches.get_one("id").unwrap();
299	        storage::delete(id)?;
300	        Ok(Output::Silent)
301	    });
302	
303	    // 3. Create hooks
304	    let hooks = Hooks::new()
305	        .pre_dispatch(|_m, _ctx| {
306	            println!("Starting command...");
307	            Ok(())
308	        });
309	
310	    // 4. Parse and dispatch
311	    let matches = cmd.get_matches();
312	    let path = extract_command_path(&matches);
313	    let mut ctx = CommandContext {
314	        command_path: path.clone(),
315	        ..Default::default()
316	    };
317	
318	    // Run pre-dispatch hooks (may inject state via ctx.extensions)
319	    hooks.run_pre_dispatch(&matches, &mut ctx)?;
320	
321	    // Dispatch based on command
322	    let result = match path_to_string(&path).as_str() {
323	        "list" => {
324	            let output = list_handler.handle(&matches, &ctx)?;
325	            if let Output::Render(data) = output {
326	                println!("{}", serde_json::to_string_pretty(&data)?);
327	            }
328	        }
329	        "delete" => {
330	            let deep = get_deepest_matches(&matches);
331	            delete_handler.handle(deep, &ctx)?;
332	            println!("Deleted.");
333	        }
334	        _ => eprintln!("Unknown command"),
335	    };
336	
337	    Ok(())
338	}
339	```
340	
341	---
342	
343	## Summary
344	
345	The execution model provides:
346	
347	1. **Clear pipeline** — Each stage has defined inputs and outputs
348	2. **Hook points** — Intercept before, after handler, and after render
349	3. **Command routing** — Utilities for navigating subcommand hierarchies
350	4. **Presentation ownership** — Rendering stays outside dispatch handlers
351	5. **Testable stages** — Each component can be tested in isolation
352

1	# File System Resources
2	
3	`standout-render` supports file-based templates and stylesheets that can be hot-reloaded during development and embedded into release binaries. This workflow combines the rapid iteration of interpreted languages with the distribution simplicity of compiled binaries.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## The Development Workflow
8	
9	During development, you want to:
10	
11	1. Edit a template or stylesheet
12	2. Re-run your program
13	3. See changes immediately
14	
15	During release, you want:
16	
17	1. A single binary with no external dependencies
18	2. No file paths to manage
19	3. No risk of missing assets
20	
21	`standout-render` supports both modes with the same code.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Hot Reload
26	
27	In debug builds (`debug_assertions` enabled), file-based templates are re-read from disk on each render. This means:
28	
29	- Edit `templates/report.jinja` → re-run → see changes
30	- No recompilation needed
31	
32	```rust
33	use standout_render::{Renderer, Theme};
34	
35	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(Theme::new())?;
36	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
37	
38	// In debug: reads from disk each time
39	// In release: content was scanned once at registration
40	let output = renderer.render("report", &data)?;
41	```
42	
43	### How It Works
44	
45	`Renderer` tracks the source of each template name:
46	
47	- **Inline** (`add_template`) and **embedded** (`with_embedded`, `with_embedded_source`) content: always cached, never re-read.
48	- **File-based** (`add_template_dir`): path recorded; in debug builds the file is re-read before each render, so edits are visible without recompiling.
49	
50	---
51	
52	## Supported Extensions
53	
54	### Templates
55	
56	| Extension | Priority |
57	| ----------- | ---------- |
58	| `.jinja` | 1 (highest) |
59	| `.jinja2` | 2 |
60	| `.j2` | 3 |
61	| `.stpl` | 4 |
62	| `.txt` | 5 (lowest) |
63	
64	If both `report.jinja` and `report.txt` exist in the same directory, `report.jinja` is used. A lookup tries the given name exactly first; if that carries one of the extensions above, it also tries the name with that extension stripped.
65	
66	### Stylesheets
67	
68	| Extension | Format |
69	| ----------- | -------- |
70	| `.css` | CSS syntax |
71	| `.yaml` | YAML syntax |
72	| `.yml` | YAML syntax |
73	
74	---
75	
76	## Embedding Resources
77	
78	For release builds, embed resources into the binary at compile time with `embed_templates!` / `embed_styles!`. Each macro reads matching files under the given directory and returns an `EmbeddedTemplates` / `EmbeddedStyles` value (both are `EmbeddedSource<R>`, differing only in the resource kind).
79	
80	```rust
81	use standout_render::{embed_templates, embed_styles, Renderer, Theme};
82	
83	let templates = embed_templates!("src/templates");
84	let styles = embed_styles!("src/styles");
85	
86	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(Theme::new())?;
87	renderer.with_embedded_source(templates);
88	```
89	
90	`EmbeddedSource::should_hot_reload()` is `true` in debug builds when the original source directory (recorded at compile time) still exists on disk. What that buys depends on which consumer takes the value, and the two differ:
91	
92	- **`App::builder().templates(embedded)` / `.styles(embedded)`** call `EmbeddedSource::into_registry`, which under `should_hot_reload()` walks the source directory and registers the entries as **file-backed**. A debug build therefore re-reads them per render, exactly like `add_template_dir`. See the standout framework docs for that wiring.
93	- **`Renderer::with_embedded_source`** builds that registry and then copies every resolved entry in with `add_inline`. The content is **snapshotted at registration**, so a `Renderer` does not re-read the source directory afterwards — `should_hot_reload()` changes nothing a caller can observe on this path.
94	
95	### Hybrid Approach
96	
97	Combine embedded defaults with an optional file directory. The directory **adds** names; it cannot replace one, because tier 1 is consulted first (see [Resolution Priority](#resolution-priority)) and `with_embedded_source` has already put every embedded name there:
98	
99	```rust
100	use standout_render::{embed_templates, Renderer, Theme};
101	use std::path::Path;
102	
103	let embedded = embed_templates!("src/templates");
104	
105	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(Theme::new())?;
106	renderer.with_embedded_source(embedded);
107	
108	// Only reached for names not already resolved above
109	if Path::new("./templates").exists() {
110	    renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
111	}
112	```
113	
114	So `./templates` supplies templates the binary does not embed. A same-named file there is **not** an override: `render("report")` still resolves the embedded `report`. To let a directory win over the binary's copy, do not register the embedded source at all when the directory exists.
115	
116	---
117	
118	## Resolution Priority
119	
120	`Renderer` resolves a name in two tiers:
121	
122	1. **Inline and embedded** — `add_template` and `with_embedded`/`with_embedded_source` write into the same namespace. Whichever call registered a name last wins; there's no separate priority between "inline" and "embedded" content.
123	2. **File-based directories** (`add_template_dir`) — checked only for a name not already resolved in tier 1.
124	
125	Registering the **same name from two different directories is a collision error**, not a silent override — file-based names must be unique across every directory you register.
126	
127	```rust
128	renderer.with_embedded_source(embedded);   // Tier 1
129	renderer.add_template("report", "inline"); // Tier 1 — overwrites "report" if embedded also defined it
130	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?; // Tier 2 — only used for names tier 1 doesn't have
131	```
132	
133	---
134	
135	## Directory Structure
136	
137	Recommended project layout:
138	
139	```text
140	my-cli/
141	├── src/
142	│   ├── main.rs
143	│   ├── templates/           # Templates for embedding
144	│   │   ├── list.jinja
145	│   │   ├── detail.jinja
146	│   │   └── partials/
147	│   │       └── header.jinja
148	│   └── styles/              # Stylesheets for embedding
149	│       ├── default.css
150	│       └── colorblind.css
151	├── templates/               # Extra development templates (gitignored)
152	└── styles/                  # Extra development stylesheets (gitignored)
153	```
154	
155	In `main.rs`:
156	
157	```rust
158	use std::path::Path;
159	
160	let embedded_templates = embed_templates!("src/templates");
161	
162	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(theme)?;
163	renderer.with_embedded_source(embedded_templates);
164	
165	// In debug, also pick up local templates the binary does not embed.
166	// Names the binary already embeds keep resolving to the embedded copy.
167	#[cfg(debug_assertions)]
168	{
169	    if Path::new("./templates").exists() {
170	        renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
171	    }
172	}
173	```
174	
175	---
176	
177	## Error Handling
178	
179	### Missing Templates
180	
181	```rust
182	match renderer.render("nonexistent", &data) {
183	    Ok(output) => println!("{}", output),
184	    Err(e) => {
185	        // Template not found in any source
186	        eprintln!("Template error: {}", e);
187	    }
188	}
189	```
190	
191	### Name Collisions
192	
193	Same-directory collisions use extension priority (`.jinja` beats `.txt`, etc. — see the table above).
194	
195	Collisions across two different directories registered with `add_template_dir` are reported as `RegistryError::Collision`, not silently resolved by registration order.
196	
197	### Invalid Content
198	
199	Template syntax errors are reported with the template name and the underlying engine's message.
200	
201	---
202	
203	## API Reference
204	
205	### Renderer
206	
207	The primary entry point for most applications:
208	
209	```rust
210	use standout_render::{Renderer, Theme};
211	
212	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(Theme::new())?;
213	
214	// Templates
215	renderer.add_template("name", "content")?;
216	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
217	renderer.with_embedded_source(embed_templates!("src/templates"));
218	
219	// Render
220	let output = renderer.render("name", &data)?;
221	let count = renderer.template_count();
222	```
223	
224	### TemplateRegistry
225	
226	The lower-level registry `Renderer` builds on internally. Use it directly only when bypassing `Renderer`:
227	
228	```rust
229	use standout_render::TemplateRegistry;
230	
231	let mut registry = TemplateRegistry::new();
232	
233	registry.add_inline("greeting", "Hello, {{ name }}!");
234	registry.add_embedded(embedded_map); // HashMap<String, String>
235	
236	// Query — `get` returns the resolved source, not the raw content
237	let resolved = registry.get("greeting")?;   // Result<ResolvedTemplate, RegistryError>
238	let content = registry.get_content("greeting")?; // Result<String, RegistryError>
239	let names: Vec<&str> = registry.names().collect();
240	```
241	
242	### StylesheetRegistry
243	
244	```rust
245	use standout_render::StylesheetRegistry;
246	
247	let mut registry = StylesheetRegistry::new();
248	registry.add_dir("./styles")?;
249	registry.add_embedded(embedded_themes); // HashMap<String, Theme>
250	
251	let theme = registry.get("default")?;      // Result<Theme, StylesheetError>
252	let exists: bool = registry.contains("default");
253	let names: Vec<&str> = registry.names().collect();
254	```
255	
256	### Embed Macros
257	
258	```rust
259	use standout_render::{embed_templates, embed_styles};
260	
261	// At compile time, reads all matching files and embeds their content
262	let templates = embed_templates!("path/to/templates");
263	let styles = embed_styles!("path/to/styles");
264	```

# Passthrough Commands

Every other way of registering a command — the `Dispatch` derive,
`command_with`, a `#[handler]` function — assumes the handler hands back
something serializable that Standout can render or serialize. A passthrough
command is the one registration shape without that assumption: the handler
writes its own bytes and returns `Result<(), anyhow::Error>`. ADR-0032 keeps
it as a secondary path for that reason: nothing else on the registration axis
accepts a signature with no serializable output and no render.

Reach for it when a command's job is genuinely "run this external process and
let it own the terminal" — streaming a subprocess's output live, driving an
interactive prompt library that writes ANSI itself, or wrapping a tool that
already produces its own formatted output — not for handlers that happen to
print instead of returning data.

## API

```rust
impl AppBuilder {
    pub fn command_passthrough<F>(self, path: &str, handler: F) -> Result<Self, SetupError>
    where
        F: FnMut(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> + 'static;
}
```

For a command declared inside `.commands(|g| ...)`, `GroupBuilder` has the
matching entry point:

```rust
impl GroupBuilder {
    pub fn passthrough<F>(self, name: &str, handler: F) -> Self
    where
        F: FnMut(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> + 'static;
}
```

Both take the same closure shape and register the command with no template:
there is nothing for a template to render.

## What it does not get

A passthrough command has no `Output` enum to return, so it gets none of the
things that come from having one:

- No template. The command is registered with its template reference set to
  "absent, silently" — there is no configured or conventional template to
  resolve, by design, not by omission.
- No render pass, so no theme, no style tags, no `Tabular` columns.
- No structured output modes. `Output::Render` is what `--output json` (and
  `yaml`/`xml`/`csv`) serializes; a passthrough handler never produces an
  `Output` value, so those modes have nothing to act on.
- No post-dispatch hooks. The passthrough dispatch closure is handed the
  command's `Hooks` and ignores them, so nothing runs between the handler
  returning and the empty result leaving dispatch.

App-level hooks registered for the command's path *do* still run, because they
sit outside the dispatch closure: a pre-dispatch hook runs before the handler
as it would for any command, and a post-output hook runs after it, receiving
`RenderedOutput::Silent`. A post-output hook attached to a passthrough command
is therefore not inert — it observes and can act, it just has no rendered text
to transform.

Concretely, under `--output json` (or any other output mode) a passthrough
command runs exactly the same as under the default: the dispatch closure
backing `command_passthrough`/`passthrough` takes the output mode as a
parameter and ignores it. Standout's own output-writing pipeline resolves the
command to an empty string every time — whatever the handler wrote, it wrote
directly (to stdout, stderr, a file, wherever), outside that pipeline, and
`--output` has no way to reach it.

## What the handler is responsible for

Because nothing downstream will format or emit anything on the handler's
behalf, the handler owns:

- Writing everything it wants seen — to stdout, stderr, or elsewhere.
- Its own error reporting for anything it prints before returning `Err(...)`;
  the `anyhow::Error` becomes the command's failure, but text already written
  stays written.
- Respecting (or explicitly ignoring) the user's terminal — colors, width,
  paging — since none of the framework's rendering machinery runs.

## Worked example

```rust
use anyhow::Context;
use clap::ArgMatches;
use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext};
use std::process::Command;

fn run_migrations(_matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
    let status = Command::new("./migrate.sh")
        .status()
        .context("failed to launch migrate.sh")?;
    if !status.success() {
        anyhow::bail!("migrate.sh exited with {status}");
    }
    Ok(())
}

let app = App::builder()
    .command_passthrough("migrate", run_migrations)?
    .build()?;
```

`migrate.sh`'s own stdout and stderr reach the terminal unchanged; Standout
neither captures nor reformats them.

## When not to use it

The blessed path is a `#[handler]` function returning `Result<T, E>`, wrapped
in `Output::Render` and rendered through a template — see
[Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md). Reach for
that whenever the command has any data a caller might want as JSON, any
output a template could format, or any reason to support `--output`. Use
passthrough only when the handler's whole job is to hand control to
something else that already owns its own bytes.

content.content:
1	# Output Modes
2	
3	Standout supports multiple output formats through a single handler because modern CLI tools serve two masters: human operators and machine automation.
4	
5	The same handler logic produces styled terminal output for eyes, plain text for logs, or structured JSON for `jq` pipelines—controlled entirely by the user's `--output` flag. This frees you from writing separate "API" and "CLI" logic.
6	
7	## The OutputMode Enum
8	
9	```rust
10	pub enum OutputMode {
11	    Auto,       // Auto-detect terminal capabilities
12	    Term,       // Always use ANSI escape codes
13	    Text,       // Never use ANSI codes (plain text)
14	    TermDebug,  // Keep style tags as [name]...[/name]
15	    Json,       // Serialize as JSON (skip template)
16	    Yaml,       // Serialize as YAML (skip template)
17	    Xml,        // Serialize as XML (skip template)
18	    Csv,        // Serialize as CSV (skip template)
19	}
20	```
21	
22	Three categories:
23	
24	**Templated modes** (Auto, Term, Text): Render the template, vary ANSI handling.
25	
26	**Debug mode** (TermDebug): Render the template, keep tags as literals for inspection.
27	
28	**Structured modes** (Json, Yaml, Xml, Csv): Skip the template entirely, serialize handler data directly.
29	
30	## Auto Mode
31	
32	`Auto` is the default. It queries the terminal for color support:
33	
34	```rust
35	Term::stdout().features().colors_supported()
36	```
37	
38	If colors are supported, Auto behaves like Term (ANSI codes applied). If not, Auto behaves like Text (tags stripped).
39	
40	This detection happens at render time, not startup. Piping output to a file or another process typically disables color support, so:
41	
42	```bash
43	myapp list              # Colors (if terminal supports)
44	myapp list > file.txt   # No colors (not a TTY)
45	myapp list | less       # No colors (pipe)
46	```
47	
48	## The --output Flag
49	
50	Standout adds a global `--output` flag accepting these values:
51	
52	```bash
53	myapp list --output=auto        # Default
54	myapp list --output=term        # Force ANSI codes
55	myapp list --output=text        # Force plain text
56	myapp list --output=term-debug  # Show style tags
57	myapp list --output=json        # JSON serialization
58	myapp list --output=yaml        # YAML serialization
59	myapp list --output=xml         # XML serialization
60	myapp list --output=csv         # CSV serialization
61	```
62	
63	The flag is global—it applies to all subcommands.
64	
65	## Term vs Text
66	
67	**Term**: turns every resolved style tag into ANSI escape codes, including
68	when the destination is a pipe rather than a terminal:
69	
70	```bash
71	myapp list --output=term > colored.txt
72	```
73	
74	Useful when you want to preserve colors for later display (e.g., `less -R`).
75	
76	A `term` request is unconditional, and the environment's color conventions do
77	not override it: `NO_COLOR=1 myapp list --output=term` still emits ANSI, the
78	same way `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 myapp list --output=text` still emits none. `auto`
79	is the only mode the environment reaches, and it reaches it through one value:
80	the destination's reported color capability. `auto` resolves to `term` when
81	that capability is reported and to `text` when it is not. `NO_COLOR` and
82	`TERM=dumb` suppress the capability, so they turn `auto` plain;
83	`CLICOLOR_FORCE` is not part of that capability probe, so it never turns `auto`
84	into `term`.
85	
86	**Text**: removes Standout's own style tags and adds no ANSI of its own:
87	
88	```bash
89	myapp list --output=text
90	```
91	
92	Useful for clean output regardless of terminal capabilities, or when processing output with other tools.
93	
94	Neither `term` nor `text` touches ANSI bytes that a handler or template
95	writes literally into the rendered text — the framework does not sanitize
96	those bytes and does not promise to. A caller that needs them gone strips
97	them itself.
98	
99	`term-debug` (which shows tags as `[name]...[/name]` rather than resolving
100	them) is internal: its tag vocabulary and exact spelling may change in any
101	release, so don't build automation against its output the way you might
102	against `term` or `text`.
103	
104	## TermDebug Mode
105	
106	TermDebug preserves style tags instead of converting them:
107	
108	```text
109	Template: [title]Hello[/title]
110	Output:   [title]Hello[/title]
111	```
112	
113	Use cases:
114	
115	- Debugging template issues
116	- Verifying style tag placement
117	- Automated testing of template output
118	
119	Unlike Term mode, unknown tags don't get the `?` marker in TermDebug.
120	TermDebug shows tag placement; it does not check whether a tag has a matching
121	style definition. Use `validate_template` when validation is required.
122	
123	## Structured Modes
124	
125	Structured modes bypass the template entirely. Handler data is serialized directly:
126	
127	```rust
128	#[derive(Serialize)]
129	struct ListOutput {
130	    items: Vec<Item>,
131	    total: usize,
132	}
133	
134	fn list_handler(...) -> HandlerResult<ListOutput> {
135	    Ok(Output::Render(ListOutput { items, total: items.len() }))
136	}
137	```
138	
139	```bash
140	myapp list --output=json
141	```
142	
143	```json
144	{
145	  "items": [...],
146	  "total": 42
147	}
148	```
149	
150	Same handler, same types—different output format. This enables:
151	
152	- Machine-readable output for scripts
153	- Integration with other tools (`jq`, etc.)
154	- API-like behavior from CLI apps
155	
156	### CSV Output
157	
158	Normal `App` dispatch flattens the serializable handler data automatically for
159	CSV. That is the same handler data used by the other structured modes; handlers
160	should not inspect the requested mode or return a CSV-specific shape.
161	
162	The standalone rendering API also supports direct `FlatDataSpec` rendering when
163	a caller needs explicit columns and headers:
164	
165	```rust
166	use standout::tabular::{Column, FlatDataSpec, Width};
167	use standout::OutputMode;
168	use standout_render::render_auto_with_spec;
169	
170	let spec = FlatDataSpec::builder()
171	    .column(Column::new(Width::Fixed(10)).key("name").header("Name"))
172	    .column(Column::new(Width::Fixed(10)).key("meta.role").header("Role"))
173	    .build();
174	
175	render_auto_with_spec(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Csv, Some(&spec))?
176	```
177	
178	The `key` field uses dot notation for nested paths (`"meta.role"` extracts `data["meta"]["role"]`).
179	
180	When a command's canonical response is an object containing the CSV rows,
181	attach a presentation-layer projection through `CommandConfig`:
182	
183	```rust
184	use serde_json::json;
185	use standout::cli::FnHandler;
186	use standout::tabular::{Column, Width};
187	use standout::{CsvProjection, StructuredOutputProjection};
188	
189	let projection = StructuredOutputProjection::csv(
190	    CsvProjection::builder("items")
191	        .column(Column::new(Width::default()).key("language").header("LANGUAGE"))
192	        .column(Column::new(Width::default()).key("code").header("CODE"))
193	        .derived_column(
194	            Column::new(Width::default()).header("NET"),
195	            |row, _root| json!(
196	                row["code"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)
197	                    - row["comments"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)
198	            ),
199	        )
200	        .synthetic_row(|root| json!({
201	            "language": "TOTAL",
202	            "code": root["totals"]["code"],
203	            "comments": root["totals"]["comments"]
204	        }))
205	        .conditional_row(|root| {
206	            (root["skipped"].as_u64().unwrap_or(0) > 0)
207	                .then(|| json!({ "language": "SKIPPED" }))
208	        })
209	        .build(),
210	);
211	
212	App::builder().command_with("summary", FnHandler::new(summary_handler), |config| {
213	    config.structured_output_projection(projection)
214	})?;
215	```
216	
217	Direct-column dot paths are resolved against each selected row. Derived
218	columns receive both the current row and the root response. Synthetic-row
219	callbacks receive the root response and run in registration order. Column
220	ordering, headers, and `null_repr` use the existing `FlatDataSpec` behavior.
221	
222	The projection applies only to CSV. Text and terminal modes still use the
223	template, while JSON, YAML, and XML serialize the canonical response. In the
224	pipeline, post-dispatch hooks run before projection and post-output hooks run
225	after it; `run`, `run_with`, output-file handling, and final emission
226	therefore all observe the same projected CSV.
227

# Output Modes

Standout supports multiple output formats through a single handler because modern CLI tools serve two masters: human operators and machine automation.

The same handler logic produces styled terminal output for eyes, plain text for logs, or structured JSON for `jq` pipelines—controlled entirely by the user's `--output` flag. This frees you from writing separate "API" and "CLI" logic.

## The OutputMode Enum

```rust
pub enum OutputMode {
    Auto,       // Auto-detect terminal capabilities
    Term,       // Always use ANSI escape codes
    Text,       // Never use ANSI codes (plain text)
    TermDebug,  // Keep style tags as [name]...[/name]
    Json,       // Serialize as JSON (skip template)
    Yaml,       // Serialize as YAML (skip template)
    Xml,        // Serialize as XML (skip template)
    Csv,        // Serialize as CSV (skip template)
}
```

Three categories:

**Templated modes** (Auto, Term, Text): Render the template, vary ANSI handling.

**Debug mode** (TermDebug): Render the template, keep tags as literals for inspection.

**Structured modes** (Json, Yaml, Xml, Csv): Skip the template entirely, serialize handler data directly.

## Auto Mode

`Auto` is the default. It queries the terminal for color support:

```rust
Term::stdout().features().colors_supported()
```

If colors are supported, Auto behaves like Term (ANSI codes applied). If not, Auto behaves like Text (tags stripped).

This detection happens at render time, not startup. Piping output to a file or another process typically disables color support, so:

```bash
myapp list              # Colors (if terminal supports)
myapp list > file.txt   # No colors (not a TTY)
myapp list | less       # No colors (pipe)
```

## The --output Flag

Standout adds a global `--output` flag accepting these values:

```bash
myapp list --output=auto        # Default
myapp list --output=term        # Force ANSI codes
myapp list --output=text        # Force plain text
myapp list --output=term-debug  # Show style tags
myapp list --output=json        # JSON serialization
myapp list --output=yaml        # YAML serialization
myapp list --output=xml         # XML serialization
myapp list --output=csv         # CSV serialization
```

The flag is global—it applies to all subcommands.

## Term vs Text

**Term**: turns every resolved style tag into ANSI escape codes, including
when the destination is a pipe rather than a terminal:

```bash
myapp list --output=term > colored.txt
```

Useful when you want to preserve colors for later display (e.g., `less -R`).

A `term` request is unconditional, and the environment's color conventions do
not override it: `NO_COLOR=1 myapp list --output=term` still emits ANSI, the
same way `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 myapp list --output=text` still emits none. `auto`
is the only mode the environment reaches, and it reaches it through one value:
the destination's reported color capability. `auto` resolves to `term` when
that capability is reported and to `text` when it is not. `NO_COLOR` and
`TERM=dumb` suppress the capability, so they turn `auto` plain;
`CLICOLOR_FORCE` is not part of that capability probe, so it never turns `auto`
into `term`.

**Text**: removes Standout's own style tags and adds no ANSI of its own:

```bash
myapp list --output=text
```

Useful for clean output regardless of terminal capabilities, or when processing output with other tools.

Neither `term` nor `text` touches ANSI bytes that a handler or template
writes literally into the rendered text — the framework does not sanitize
those bytes and does not promise to. A caller that needs them gone strips
them itself.

`term-debug` (which shows tags as `[name]...[/name]` rather than resolving
them) is internal: its tag vocabulary and exact spelling may change in any
release, so don't build automation against its output the way you might
against `term` or `text`.

## TermDebug Mode

TermDebug preserves style tags instead of converting them:

```text
Template: [title]Hello[/title]
Output:   [title]Hello[/title]
```

Use cases:

- Debugging template issues
- Verifying style tag placement
- Automated testing of template output

Unlike Term mode, unknown tags don't get the `?` marker in TermDebug.
TermDebug shows tag placement; it does not check whether a tag has a matching
style definition. Use `validate_template` when validation is required.

## Structured Modes

Structured modes bypass the template entirely. Handler data is serialized directly:

```rust
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ListOutput {
    items: Vec<Item>,
    total: usize,
}

fn list_handler(...) -> HandlerResult<ListOutput> {
    Ok(Output::Render(ListOutput { items, total: items.len() }))
}
```

```bash
myapp list --output=json
```

```json
{
  "items": [...],
  "total": 42
}
```

Same handler, same types—different output format. This enables:

- Machine-readable output for scripts
- Integration with other tools (`jq`, etc.)
- API-like behavior from CLI apps

### CSV Output

Normal `App` dispatch flattens the serializable handler data automatically for
CSV. That is the same handler data used by the other structured modes; handlers
should not inspect the requested mode or return a CSV-specific shape.

The standalone rendering API also supports direct `FlatDataSpec` rendering when
a caller needs explicit columns and headers:

```rust
use standout::tabular::{Column, FlatDataSpec, Width};
use standout::OutputMode;
use standout_render::render_auto_with_spec;

let spec = FlatDataSpec::builder()
    .column(Column::new(Width::Fixed(10)).key("name").header("Name"))
    .column(Column::new(Width::Fixed(10)).key("meta.role").header("Role"))
    .build();

render_auto_with_spec(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Csv, Some(&spec))?
```

The `key` field uses dot notation for nested paths (`"meta.role"` extracts `data["meta"]["role"]`).

When a command's canonical response is an object containing the CSV rows,
attach a presentation-layer projection through `CommandConfig`:

```rust
use serde_json::json;
use standout::cli::FnHandler;
use standout::tabular::{Column, Width};
use standout::{CsvProjection, StructuredOutputProjection};

let projection = StructuredOutputProjection::csv(
    CsvProjection::builder("items")
        .column(Column::new(Width::default()).key("language").header("LANGUAGE"))
        .column(Column::new(Width::default()).key("code").header("CODE"))
        .derived_column(
            Column::new(Width::default()).header("NET"),
            |row, _root| json!(
                row["code"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)
                    - row["comments"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)
            ),
        )
        .synthetic_row(|root| json!({
            "language": "TOTAL",
            "code": root["totals"]["code"],
            "comments": root["totals"]["comments"]
        }))
        .conditional_row(|root| {
            (root["skipped"].as_u64().unwrap_or(0) > 0)
                .then(|| json!({ "language": "SKIPPED" }))
        })
        .build(),
);

App::builder().command_with("summary", FnHandler::new(summary_handler), |config| {
    config.structured_output_projection(projection)
})?;
```

Direct-column dot paths are resolved against each selected row. Derived
columns receive both the current row and the root response. Synthetic-row
callbacks receive the root response and run in registration order. Column
ordering, headers, and `null_repr` use the existing `FlatDataSpec` behavior.

The projection applies only to CSV. Text and terminal modes still use the
template, while JSON, YAML, and XML serialize the canonical response. In the
pipeline, post-dispatch hooks run before projection and post-output hooks run
after it; `run`, `run_with`, output-file handling, and final emission
therefore all observe the same projected CSV.

See [Introduction to Tabular](../crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md) for
tabular specifications and layout.

## File Output

The `--output-file-path` flag redirects output to a file:

```bash
myapp list --output-file-path=results.txt
myapp list --output=json --output-file-path=data.json
```

Behavior:

- Text output: written to file, nothing printed to stdout
- Binary output: written to the requested file instead of stdout
- Silent output: no-op

After writing to file, stdout output is suppressed to prevent double-printing.

## Customizing Flags

Rename or disable the flags via `AppBuilder`:

```rust
App::builder()
    .output_flag(Some("format"))       // --format instead of --output
    .output_file_flag(Some("out"))     // --out instead of --output-file-path
    .build()?
```

```rust
App::builder()
    .no_output_flag()                  // Disable --output entirely
    .no_output_file_flag()             // Disable file output
    .build()?
```

## Keep Output Mode Out of Handlers

Output mode is a rendering concern and is deliberately absent from
`CommandContext`. A handler should return the same serializable data regardless
of whether the caller selected terminal, text, or structured output. If a
command's behavior genuinely differs, model that as an explicit command or
argument rather than an implicit presentation-mode branch.

## Rendering Without CLI

For standalone rendering with explicit mode:

```rust
use standout::{render_auto, OutputMode};

// Renders template for Term/Text, serializes for Json/Yaml
let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
```

The "auto" in `render_auto` refers to template-vs-serialize dispatch, not color detection.

For full control over both output mode and color mode:

```rust
use standout::{render_with_mode, ColorMode};

let output = render_with_mode(
    template,
    &data,
    &theme,
    OutputMode::Term,
    ColorMode::Dark,
)?;
```

1	# Template Engines
2	
3	`standout-render` uses a pluggable template engine architecture. While MiniJinja is the default (and recommended for most users), you can choose a lighter engine or implement your own.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Available Engines
8	
9	| Engine            | Syntax      | Features                               | Binary Size | Use When                             |
10	| ----------------- | ----------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------ |
11	| `MiniJinjaEngine` | `{{ var }}` | Loops, conditionals, filters, includes | ~248KB      | Full template logic needed (default) |
12	| `SimpleEngine`    | `{var}`     | Variable substitution only             | ~5KB        | Simple output, minimal binary size   |
13	
14	### Feature Comparison
15	
16	| Feature                       | MiniJinjaEngine                | SimpleEngine       |
17	| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------ |
18	| Variable substitution         | `{{ name }}`                   | `{name}`           |
19	| Nested property access        | `{{ user.name }}`              | `{user.name}`      |
20	| Array index access            | `{{ items[0] }}`               | `{items.0}`        |
21	| Filters                       | `{{ name \| upper }}`          | -                  |
22	| Conditionals                  | `{% if %}...{% endif %}`       | -                  |
23	| Loops                         | `{% for %}...{% endfor %}`     | -                  |
24	| Template includes             | `{% include "file" %}`         | -                  |
25	| Macros                        | `{% macro %}...{% endmacro %}` | -                  |
26	| Comments                      | `{# comment #}`                | -                  |
27	| Escaped delimiters            | `{{ "{{" }}`                   | `{{` → `{`         |
28	| Context injection             | Yes                            | Yes                |
29	| Named templates               | Yes                            | Yes                |
30	| Style tags                    | Yes (pass-through)             | Yes (pass-through) |
31	| Hot reload                    | Yes                            | Yes                |
32	| Structured output (JSON/YAML) | Yes                            | Yes                |
33	
34	### MiniJinjaEngine (Default)
35	
36	Full-featured Jinja2-compatible engine. This is what you get by default.
37	
38	```jinja
39	[title]{{ name | upper }}[/title]
40	{% for item in items %}
41	  {{ loop.index }}. {{ item.name }}
42	{% endfor %}
43	```
44	
45	**Supports:**
46	
47	- Variable substitution with filters: `{{ name | upper }}`
48	- Control flow: `{% if %}`, `{% for %}`, `{% macro %}`
49	- Template includes: `{% include "partial.jinja" %}`
50	- Custom filters and functions
51	
52	**File extensions:** `.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`
53	
54	### SimpleEngine
55	
56	Lightweight engine using format-string style syntax. No loops, conditionals, or filters.
57	
58	```text
59	[title]{name}[/title]
60	Status: {status}
61	Contact: {user.profile.email}
62	```
63	
64	**Supports:**
65	
66	- Simple variable substitution: `{name}`
67	- Nested property access: `{user.profile.email}`
68	- Array index access: `{items.0}`
69	- Escaped braces: `{{` renders as `{`
70	
71	**Does NOT support:**
72	
73	- Loops (`{% for %}`)
74	- Conditionals (`{% if %}`)
75	- Filters (`| upper`)
76	- Template includes
77	
78	**File extension:** `.stpl`
79	
80	---
81	
82	## Choosing an Engine
83	
84	### Use MiniJinjaEngine (default) when
85	
86	- Templates need loops or conditionals
87	- You use filters for formatting
88	- Templates include other templates
89	- You're not concerned about binary size
90	
91	### Use SimpleEngine when
92	
93	- Templates only substitute variables
94	- Binary size is critical
95	- You want faster parsing (no template compilation)
96	- Templates are simple status messages or one-liners
97	
98	---
99	
100	## Using SimpleEngine
101	
102	### With Renderer
103	
104	```rust
105	use standout_render::{Renderer, Theme, OutputMode};
106	use standout_render::template::SimpleEngine;
107	
108	let engine = Box::new(SimpleEngine::new());
109	let mut renderer = Renderer::with_output_and_engine(
110	    Theme::new(),
111	    OutputMode::Auto,
112	    engine,
113	)?;
114	
115	renderer.add_template("status", "Status: {status}, Count: {count}")?;
116	
117	let output = renderer.render("status", &data)?;
118	```
119	
120	### With render_auto_with_engine
121	
122	```rust
123	use standout_render::{render_auto_with_engine, Theme, OutputMode};
124	use standout_render::template::SimpleEngine;
125	use standout_render::context::{ContextRegistry, RenderContext};
126	
127	let engine = SimpleEngine::new();
128	let theme = Theme::new();
129	let data = serde_json::json!({"name": "World"});
130	
131	let registry = ContextRegistry::new();
132	let render_ctx = RenderContext::new(OutputMode::Text, Some(80), &theme, &data);
133	
134	let output = render_auto_with_engine(
135	    &engine,
136	    "Hello, {name}!",
137	    &data,
138	    &theme,
139	    OutputMode::Text,
140	    &registry,
141	    &render_ctx,
142	)?;
143	```
144	
145	---
146	
147	## File Extension Mapping
148	
149	When loading templates from files, the extension determines the intended engine:
150	
151	| Priority | Extension | Engine          |
152	| -------- | --------- | --------------- |
153	| 1        | `.jinja`  | MiniJinjaEngine |
154	| 2        | `.jinja2` | MiniJinjaEngine |
155	| 3        | `.j2`     | MiniJinjaEngine |
156	| 4        | `.stpl`   | SimpleEngine    |
157	| 5        | `.txt`    | (generic)       |
158	
159	When multiple files share the same base name, higher-priority extensions win for extensionless lookups.
160	
161	**Note:** The registry resolves templates by name, but doesn't automatically select the engine. You must configure the appropriate engine when creating the `Renderer`.
162	
163	---
164	
165	## Implementing a Custom Engine
166	
167	To create your own template engine, implement the `TemplateEngine` trait:
168	
169	```rust
170	use standout_render::template::TemplateEngine;
171	use standout_render::RenderError;
172	use std::collections::HashMap;
173	
174	pub struct MyEngine {
175	    templates: HashMap<String, String>,
176	}
177	
178	impl TemplateEngine for MyEngine {
179	    fn render_template(
180	        &self,
181	        template: &str,
182	        data: &serde_json::Value,
183	    ) -> Result<String, RenderError> {
184	        // Your rendering logic here
185	        Ok(format!("Rendered: {}", template))
186	    }
187	
188	    fn add_template(&mut self, name: &str, source: &str) -> Result<(), RenderError> {
189	        self.templates.insert(name.to_string(), source.to_string());
190	        Ok(())
191	    }
192	
193	    fn render_named(
194	        &self,
195	        name: &str,
196	        data: &serde_json::Value,
197	    ) -> Result<String, RenderError> {
198	        let template = self.templates.get(name)
199	            .ok_or_else(|| RenderError::TemplateNotFound(name.to_string()))?;
200	        self.render_template(template, data)
201	    }
202	
203	    fn has_template(&self, name: &str) -> bool {
204	        self.templates.contains_key(name)
205	    }
206	
207	    fn render_with_context(
208	        &self,
209	        template: &str,
210	        data: &serde_json::Value,
211	        context: HashMap<String, serde_json::Value>,
212	    ) -> Result<String, RenderError> {
213	        // Merge context with data and render
214	        self.render_template(template, data)
215	    }
216	
217	    fn supports_includes(&self) -> bool { false }
218	    fn supports_filters(&self) -> bool { false }
219	    fn supports_control_flow(&self) -> bool { false }
220	}
221	```
222	
223	### Trait Methods
224	
225	| Method                | Purpose                                  |
226	| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
227	| `render_template`     | Render an inline template string         |
228	| `add_template`        | Register a named template                |
229	| `render_named`        | Render a previously registered template  |
230	| `has_template`        | Check if a template exists               |
231	| `render_with_context` | Render with additional context variables |
232	| `supports_*`          | Feature flags for capability discovery   |
233	
234	---
235	
236	## API Reference
237	
238	### Engine Types
239	
240	```rust
241	use standout_render::template::{
242	    TemplateEngine,      // Trait for all engines
243	    MiniJinjaEngine,     // Default, full-featured
244	    SimpleEngine,        // Lightweight alternative
245	};
246	```
247	
248	### Renderer with Custom Engine
249	
250	```rust
251	use standout_render::{Renderer, Theme, OutputMode};
252	
253	// Default (MiniJinja)
254	let renderer = Renderer::new(theme)?;
255	
256	// With explicit engine
257	let engine = Box::new(SimpleEngine::new());
258	let renderer = Renderer::with_output_and_engine(theme, mode, engine)?;
259	```
260	
261	### Standalone Rendering
262	
263	```rust
264	use standout_render::{
265	    render_auto_with_engine,  // Render with custom engine
266	};
267	```
268	
269	---
270	
271	## Migration Notes
272	
273	If you're upgrading from a version before pluggable engines:
274	
275	- **No changes required** - MiniJinja remains the default
276	- **Error type changed** - `minijinja::Error` is now `RenderError`
277	- **New capability** - You can now inject custom engines via `with_output_and_engine()`
278	
279	```rust
280	// Before
281	use minijinja::Error;
282	
283	// After
284	use standout_render::RenderError;
285	```
286

1	# Execution Outcomes
2	
3	Standout carries shell semantics as typed data from argument parsing through
4	dispatch, rendering, hooks, output files, and final writes. Applications can let
5	`App::run` own output without losing the distinction between a usage error and a
6	runtime failure.
7	
8	## Status and streams
9	
10	| Outcome | Stream used by `run()` | Status |
11	| --- | --- | --- |
12	| Help or version | stdout | `0` |
13	| Successful rendered text or binary | stdout | `0` |
14	| `Output::Silent` | none | `0` |
15	| `--output-file-path` success | file only | `0` |
16	| Artifact written to a file | bytes to the file, report to stdout | `0` |
17	| Artifact written to stdout | bytes to stdout, report to stderr | `0` |
18	| Artifact with no selectable destination | stderr | `1` |
19	| Clap usage error | stderr | `2` |
20	| Handler, hook, render, pipe, or write failure | stderr | `1` |
21	| Application-declared external failure | stderr | exact declared nonzero status |
22	
23	Framework warning flushing happens after the primary output and does not replace
24	its status. Warnings cover non-fatal framework-owned setup, resource-loading,
25	and accepted-input diagnostics, including answer-sheet parse warnings that do
26	not reject a questionnaire submission. A final text or binary write failure does
27	replace a successful status with `1`, except that `BrokenPipe` while writing
28	final rendered command text to stdout is successful early consumer termination.
29	
30	## Capturing typed metadata
31	
32	`run_with` keeps output in-process and returns `CompletedRun`: the dispatch
33	outcome plus any framework warnings collected during the run. `Deref` keeps
34	string-oriented accessors and typed methods (`exit_status()`, `success_kind()`,
35	`error_kind()`) working on the wrapper. Pattern matching needs `outcome()` or
36	`into_outcome()`, because `CompletedRun` is not the variant enum.
37	
38	```rust
39	use standout::cli::{
40	    CompletedRun, DispatchResult, ExitStatus, OutputKind, RunError, RunErrorKind, SuccessKind,
41	};
42	use standout::{InputSources, TargetProperties};
43	
44	let result = app.run_with(
45	    command,
46	    args,
47	    TargetProperties::detect(),
48	    InputSources::from_process(),
49	);
50	let _ = result.warnings();
51	
52	match result.outcome() {
53	    DispatchResult::Handled(output) => println!("{}", output),
54	    DispatchResult::Binary(bytes, filename) => consume(bytes, filename),
55	    DispatchResult::Artifact(run) => {
56	        use std::io::{self, Write};
57	        if run.destination().is_stdout() {
58	            let mut stdout = io::stdout();
59	            stdout.write_all(run.bytes()).and_then(|()| stdout.flush()).map_err(|error| {
60	                RunError::new(
61	                    format!("Error writing artifact stdout: {}", error),
62	                    RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
63	                )
64	            })?;
65	            if let Some(report) = run.report().filter(|r| !r.is_empty()) {
66	                let mut stderr = io::stderr();
67	                writeln!(stderr, "{}", report).and_then(|()| stderr.flush()).map_err(|error| {
68	                    RunError::new(
69	                        format!("Error writing artifact report: {}", error),
70	                        RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
71	                    )
72	                })?;
73	            }
74	        } else if let Some(report) = run.report().filter(|r| !r.is_empty()) {
75	            let mut stdout = io::stdout();
76	            writeln!(stdout, "{}", report).and_then(|()| stdout.flush()).map_err(|error| {
77	                RunError::new(
78	                    format!("Error writing artifact report: {}", error),
79	                    RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
80	                )
81	            })?;
82	        }
83	    }
84	    DispatchResult::Error(error) => eprintln!("{}", error),
85	    DispatchResult::NoMatch(_matches) => {}
86	    DispatchResult::Silent => {}
87	    _ => {}
88	}
89	
90	assert_eq!(result.exit_status(), Some(ExitStatus::SUCCESS));
91	assert_eq!(result.success_kind(), Some(SuccessKind::Command));
92	assert_eq!(result.error_kind(), None);
93	```
94	
95	Use `into_outcome()` when the fallback needs owned `ArgMatches`
96	(`DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches)`).
97	
98	`RunOutput` and `RunError` dereference to `str`, implement `Display`, and expose
99	`as_str()` / `into_string()` for callers that used the tuple payloads as text.
100	`RunOutput::kind()` names a success the same way: `Command` for a handler's
101	output, `ClapHelp` / `ClapVersion` for a help or version display, and
102	`PagedHelp` for a `help --page` display — the text is identical, but the kind
103	tells a printing caller the user asked for a pager.
104	`RunError::kind()` identifies `ClapUsage`, `Handler`, `Hook(phase)`, `Render`, or
105	`FinalWrite(Text|Binary|Artifact)`. `External` identifies the narrow
106	application-declared external path; its `exit_status()` is the exact declared
107	nonzero status and its text is the verbatim diagnostic payload.
108	
109	## No-match is a handoff, not an error
110	
111	`DispatchResult::NoMatch` retains the parsed `ArgMatches` for partial adoption. It has
112	no framework exit status: `exit_status()` returns `None`, `run()` returns
113	`false`, and Standout emits nothing. The fallback dispatcher still owns that
114	command and its eventual status.
115	
116	The reverse direction never hands off. Before parsing, `run` and
117	`run_with` check every registered path against the clap `Command`: a
118	handler registered under a path the CLI declares no subcommand for is
119	unreachable — no invocation can name it and no fallback owns it, since the app
120	did register a handler. That returns `DispatchResult::Error` naming the
121	registered path, and the clap spelling too when the two differ only by `-`
122	versus `_` (`list_units` registered against a CLI declaring `list-units`).
123	`App::verify_command` reports the same mismatch at setup time.
124	
125	That check reads canonical command names only. Clap resolves an alias to the
126	command it names before `ArgMatches` reports it, so dispatch never sees the
127	alias: a handler registered as `ls` against `Command::new("list").alias("ls")`
128	is reached by neither spelling and is reported as unreachable. Registering
129	`list` is what makes both `list` and `ls` run the handler.
130	
131	## Framework-owned final writes
132	
133	`run()` writes successful text and binary bytes to stdout, diagnostics to
134	stderr, and exits with the typed non-zero status when execution fails. The one
135	exception is a paged help display (`SuccessKind::PagedHelp`), which goes to the
136	pager instead; if no pager is available it falls back to stdout, so help is
137	never lost. A closed
138	downstream pipe is not an error only for final rendered command text:
139	`BrokenPipe` there means the consumer stopped reading early. Binary stdout
140	writes and artifact report writes keep their typed final-write failures. The
141	suggested filename on binary output remains available to capture callers; use
142	`--output-file-path` when the framework should write either text or binary to a
143	file instead of stdout.
144	
145	Capture APIs do not perform the final stdout/stderr write, but file redirection
146	is part of dispatch and therefore reports typed `FinalWrite` failures directly.
147	External failures are never redirected to an output file: they remain stderr
148	diagnostics when `run()` performs the final write.

150	Capture-mode runs drain framework warnings instead of rendering them. The raw
151	capture path stores the batch in `standout-render`'s warning collector, and
152	`standout-test::TestHarness` exposes the batch through `TestResult::warnings()`

154	
155	## Compound artifacts
156	
157	`Output::Artifact` extends the framework-owned write to commands that also have
158	something to say about it. The application returns bytes, an optional suggested
159	destination, and an optional report; Standout selects the destination, writes,

161	Ordering is the guarantee: a failed write produces `FinalWrite(Artifact)` and no

# Execution Outcomes

Standout carries shell semantics as typed data from argument parsing through
dispatch, rendering, hooks, output files, and final writes. Applications can let
`App::run` own output without losing the distinction between a usage error and a
runtime failure.

## Status and streams

| Outcome | Stream used by `run()` | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Help or version | stdout | `0` |
| Successful rendered text or binary | stdout | `0` |
| `Output::Silent` | none | `0` |
| `--output-file-path` success | file only | `0` |
| Artifact written to a file | bytes to the file, report to stdout | `0` |
| Artifact written to stdout | bytes to stdout, report to stderr | `0` |
| Artifact with no selectable destination | stderr | `1` |
| Clap usage error | stderr | `2` |
| Handler, hook, render, pipe, or write failure | stderr | `1` |
| Application-declared external failure | stderr | exact declared nonzero status |

Framework warning flushing happens after the primary output and does not replace
its status. Warnings cover non-fatal framework-owned setup, resource-loading,
and accepted-input diagnostics, including answer-sheet parse warnings that do
not reject a questionnaire submission. A final text or binary write failure does
replace a successful status with `1`, except that `BrokenPipe` while writing
final rendered command text to stdout is successful early consumer termination.

## Capturing typed metadata

`run_with` keeps output in-process and returns `CompletedRun`: the dispatch
outcome plus any framework warnings collected during the run. `Deref` keeps
string-oriented accessors and typed methods (`exit_status()`, `success_kind()`,
`error_kind()`) working on the wrapper. Pattern matching needs `outcome()` or
`into_outcome()`, because `CompletedRun` is not the variant enum.

```rust
use standout::cli::{
    CompletedRun, DispatchResult, ExitStatus, OutputKind, RunError, RunErrorKind, SuccessKind,
};
use standout::{InputSources, TargetProperties};

let result = app.run_with(
    command,
    args,
    TargetProperties::detect(),
    InputSources::from_process(),
);
let _ = result.warnings();

match result.outcome() {
    DispatchResult::Handled(output) => println!("{}", output),
    DispatchResult::Binary(bytes, filename) => consume(bytes, filename),
    DispatchResult::Artifact(run) => {
        use std::io::{self, Write};
        if run.destination().is_stdout() {
            let mut stdout = io::stdout();
            stdout.write_all(run.bytes()).and_then(|()| stdout.flush()).map_err(|error| {
                RunError::new(
                    format!("Error writing artifact stdout: {}", error),
                    RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
                )
            })?;
            if let Some(report) = run.report().filter(|r| !r.is_empty()) {
                let mut stderr = io::stderr();
                writeln!(stderr, "{}", report).and_then(|()| stderr.flush()).map_err(|error| {
                    RunError::new(
                        format!("Error writing artifact report: {}", error),
                        RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
                    )
                })?;
            }
        } else if let Some(report) = run.report().filter(|r| !r.is_empty()) {
            let mut stdout = io::stdout();
            writeln!(stdout, "{}", report).and_then(|()| stdout.flush()).map_err(|error| {
                RunError::new(
                    format!("Error writing artifact report: {}", error),
                    RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
                )
            })?;
        }
    }
    DispatchResult::Error(error) => eprintln!("{}", error),
    DispatchResult::NoMatch(_matches) => {}
    DispatchResult::Silent => {}
    _ => {}
}

assert_eq!(result.exit_status(), Some(ExitStatus::SUCCESS));
assert_eq!(result.success_kind(), Some(SuccessKind::Command));
assert_eq!(result.error_kind(), None);
```

Use `into_outcome()` when the fallback needs owned `ArgMatches`
(`DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches)`).

`RunOutput` and `RunError` dereference to `str`, implement `Display`, and expose
`as_str()` / `into_string()` for callers that used the tuple payloads as text.
`RunOutput::kind()` names a success the same way: `Command` for a handler's
output, `ClapHelp` / `ClapVersion` for a help or version display, and
`PagedHelp` for a `help --page` display — the text is identical, but the kind
tells a printing caller the user asked for a pager.
`RunError::kind()` identifies `ClapUsage`, `Handler`, `Hook(phase)`, `Render`, or
`FinalWrite(Text|Binary|Artifact)`. `External` identifies the narrow
application-declared external path; its `exit_status()` is the exact declared
nonzero status and its text is the verbatim diagnostic payload.

## No-match is a handoff, not an error

`DispatchResult::NoMatch` retains the parsed `ArgMatches` for partial adoption. It has
no framework exit status: `exit_status()` returns `None`, `run()` returns
`false`, and Standout emits nothing. The fallback dispatcher still owns that
command and its eventual status.

The reverse direction never hands off. Before parsing, `run` and
`run_with` check every registered path against the clap `Command`: a
handler registered under a path the CLI declares no subcommand for is
unreachable — no invocation can name it and no fallback owns it, since the app
did register a handler. That returns `DispatchResult::Error` naming the
registered path, and the clap spelling too when the two differ only by `-`
versus `_` (`list_units` registered against a CLI declaring `list-units`).
`App::verify_command` reports the same mismatch at setup time.

That check reads canonical command names only. Clap resolves an alias to the
command it names before `ArgMatches` reports it, so dispatch never sees the
alias: a handler registered as `ls` against `Command::new("list").alias("ls")`
is reached by neither spelling and is reported as unreachable. Registering
`list` is what makes both `list` and `ls` run the handler.

## Framework-owned final writes

`run()` writes successful text and binary bytes to stdout, diagnostics to
stderr, and exits with the typed non-zero status when execution fails. The one
exception is a paged help display (`SuccessKind::PagedHelp`), which goes to the
pager instead; if no pager is available it falls back to stdout, so help is
never lost. A closed
downstream pipe is not an error only for final rendered command text:
`BrokenPipe` there means the consumer stopped reading early. Binary stdout
writes and artifact report writes keep their typed final-write failures. The
suggested filename on binary output remains available to capture callers; use
`--output-file-path` when the framework should write either text or binary to a
file instead of stdout.

Capture APIs do not perform the final stdout/stderr write, but file redirection
is part of dispatch and therefore reports typed `FinalWrite` failures directly.
External failures are never redirected to an output file: they remain stderr
diagnostics when `run()` performs the final write.

Capture-mode runs drain framework warnings instead of rendering them. The raw
capture path stores the batch in `standout-render`'s warning collector, and
`standout-test::TestHarness` exposes the batch through `TestResult::warnings()`
so tests can assert warning content deterministically.

## Compound artifacts

`Output::Artifact` extends the framework-owned write to commands that also have
something to say about it. The application returns bytes, an optional suggested
destination, and an optional report; Standout selects the destination, writes,
and only then renders the report with a receipt naming where the bytes landed.
Ordering is the guarantee: a failed write produces `FinalWrite(Artifact)` and no
report at all, so a success message can never promise a file that never
appeared.

See [Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for the
destination policy, the report envelope, and the artifact-to-stdout report
channel.

1	# Standout How To
2	
3	This is a small, focused guide for adopting Standout in a working shell application. Each step is self-sufficient, takes a positive step towards a sane CLI design, and can be incrementally merged. This can be done for one command (probably a good idea), then replicated to as many as you'd like.
4	
5	Note that only 2 out of 8 steps are Standout related. The others are generally good practices and clear designs for maintainable shell programs. This is not an accident, as Standout's goal is to allow your app to keep a great structure effortlessly, while providing testability, rich and fast output design, and more.
6	
7	For explanation's sake, we will show a hypothetical list command for tdoo, a todo list manager.
8	
9	This guide keeps the migration in one package so each step is small. Once the
10	application behavior is separated from output, move it into a CLI-free library;
11	the canonical [production-shaped application](production-shaped-example.md)
12	shows the final ownership model.
13	
14	**See Also:**
15	
16	- [Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) - detailed handler API
17	- [App State and Extensions](../crates/dispatch/topics/app-state.md) - dependency injection patterns
18	- [Styling System](../crates/render/topics/styling-system.md) - themes and styles in depth
19	- [Output Modes](../topics/output-modes.md) - all output format options
20	- [Partial Adoption](../crates/dispatch/topics/partial-adoption.md) - migrating incrementally
21	- [Input Collection](../crates/input/guides/intro-to-input.md) - declarative input from multiple sources
22	
23	## 1. Start: The Argument Parsing
24	
25	Arg parsing is insanely intricate and deceptively simple. In case you are not already: define your application's interface with clap. Nothing else is worth doing until you have a sane starting point.
26	
27	If you don't have clap set up yet, here's a minimal starting point:
28	
29	```rust
30	use clap::{Parser, Subcommand};
31	
32	#[derive(Parser)]
33	#[command(name = "tdoo")]
34	struct Cli {
35	    #[command(subcommand)]
36	    command: Commands,
37	}
38	
39	#[derive(Subcommand)]
40	enum Commands {
41	    /// List all todos
42	    List {
43	        #[arg(short, long)]
44	        all: bool,
45	    },
46	    /// Add a new todo
47	    Add {
48	        title: String,
49	    },
50	}
51	
52	fn main() {
53	    let cli = Cli::parse();
54	    match cli.command {
55	        Commands::List { all } => list_command(all),
56	        Commands::Add { title } => add_command(&title),
57	    }
58	}
59	```
60	
61	(If you are using a non-clap-compatible crate, for now, you'd have to write an adapter for clap.)
62	
63	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` - it should compile without errors.
64	
65	## 2. Hard Split Logic and Formatting
66	
67	Now, your command should be split into two functions: the logic handler and its rendering. Don't worry about the specifics, do the straightest path from your current code.
68	
69	This is the one key step, the key design rule. And that's not because Standout requires it, rather the other way around: Standout is designed on top of it, and keeping it separate and easy to iterate on both logic and presentation under this design is Standout's key value.
70	
71	If your CLI is in good shape this will be a small task, otherwise you may find yourself patching together print statements everywhere, tidying up the data model and centralizing the processing. The silver lining here being: if it takes considerable work, there will be considerable gain in doing so.
72	
73	**Before** (tangled logic and output):
74	
75	```rust
76	fn list_command(show_all: bool) {
77	    let todos = storage::list().unwrap();
78	    println!("Your Todos:");
79	    println!("-----------");
80	    for (i, todo) in todos.iter().enumerate() {
81	        if show_all || todo.status == Status::Pending {
82	            let marker = if todo.status == Status::Done { "[x]" } else { "[ ]" };
83	            println!("{}. {} {}", i + 1, marker, todo.title);
84	        }
85	    }
86	    if todos.is_empty() {
87	        println!("No todos yet!");
88	    }
89	}
90	```
91	
92	**After** (clean separation):
93	
94	```rust
95	use clap::ArgMatches;
96	
97	// Data types for your domain
98	#[derive(Clone)]
99	pub enum Status { Pending, Done }
100	
101	#[derive(Clone)]
102	pub struct Todo {
103	    pub title: String,
104	    pub status: Status,
105	}
106	
107	pub struct TodoResult {
108	    pub message: Option<String>,
109	    pub todos: Vec<Todo>,
110	}
111	
112	// This is your application function. It knows nothing about clap and returns
113	// an ordinary Rust data type.
114	//
115	// Note: This example uses immutable references. If your application service
116	// needs mutable state (&mut self), see the "Mutable Handlers" section below.
117	pub fn list(show_done: bool) -> TodoResult {
118	    let todos = storage::list().unwrap();
119	
120	    let filtered: Vec<Todo> = if show_done {
121	        todos
122	    } else {
123	        todos.into_iter()
124	            .filter(|t| matches!(t.status, Status::Pending))
125	            .collect()
126	    };
127	
128	    TodoResult {
129	        message: None,
130	        todos: filtered,
131	    }
132	}
133	
134	// This will take the Rust data type and print the result to stdout
135	pub fn render_list(result: TodoResult) {
136	    if let Some(msg) = result.message {
137	        println!("{}", msg);
138	    }
139	    for (i, todo) in result.todos.iter().enumerate() {
140	        let status = match todo.status {
141	            Status::Done => "[x]",
142	            Status::Pending => "[ ]",
143	        };
144	        println!("{}. {} {}", i + 1, status, todo.title);
145	    }
146	}
147	
148	// And the orchestrator:
149	pub fn list_command(matches: &ArgMatches) {
150	    render_list(list(matches.get_flag("all")))
151	}
152	```
153	
154	> **Verify:** Run `cargo build` and then `tdoo list` - output should look identical to before.

175	## 3. Fine Tune the Application Result Type
176	
177	While any data type works, Standout's renderer takes a generic type that must implement `Serialize`. This enables automatic JSON/YAML output modes and template rendering through MiniJinja's context system. This is likely a small change, and beneficial as a baseline for logic results that will simplify writing renderers later.
178	
179	Add serde to your `Cargo.toml`:
180	
181	```toml
182	[dependencies]
183	serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
184	```
185	
186	Update your types:
187	
188	```rust
189	use serde::Serialize;
190	
191	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
192	#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]
193	pub enum Status { Pending, Done }
194	
195	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
196	pub struct Todo {
197	    pub title: String,
198	    pub status: Status,
199	}
200	
201	#[derive(Serialize)]
202	pub struct TodoResult {
203	    pub message: Option<String>,
204	    pub todos: Vec<Todo>,
205	}
206	```

210	## 4. Replace Imperative Print Statements With a Template
211	
212	Reading a template of an output next to the substituting variables is much easier to reason about than scattered prints, string concats and the like.
213	
214	This step is optional - if your current output is simple, you can skip to step 5. If you want an intermediate checkpoint, use Rust's format strings:
215	
216	```rust
217	pub fn render_list(result: TodoResult) {
218	    let output = format!(
219	        "{header}\n{todos}",
220	        header = result.message.unwrap_or_default(),
221	        todos = result.todos.iter().enumerate()
222	            .map(|(i, t)| format!("{}. [{}] {}", i + 1, t.status, t.title))
223	            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
224	            .join("\n")
225	    );
226	    println!("{}", output);
227	}
228	```
229	
230	> **Verify:** Run `tdoo list` - output should still work.
